#6145. American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at this elite status, and talk about what it is, how you can earn it, what the benefits are, etc. The truth is that very little is officially published about this, so we mostly have to go off of data points.

The reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines. That’s because a not-insignificant portion of the frequent flyer community finds this status to be rather “sexy,” and will go out of their way to earn it. Since the qualification requirements aren’t published, it keeps people on the hamster wheel, booking as many expensive tickets as possible.

On the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level. There’s no published criteria to earn it, and it has to be renewed every program year, so you can earn it one year and lose it the next.

Going back many years, Concierge Key was completely separate from the AAdvantage program, but that’s no longer the case. Nowadays Concierge Key is a formal part of the AAdvantage program, and it’s a tier above Executive Platinum status (American’s highest elite tier with published qualification criteria).

I think it’s also worth mentioning that Concierge Key is perhaps the most well-known invitation-only elite status in the industry, as it was a major theme of the popular 2009 movie “Up In The Air,” starring George Clooney. Ugh, I can’t believe that was over 15 years ago.

The criteria to earn Concierge Key is not published, but generally there are a few ways to earn it.

One way is to spend a ton on American Airlines travel. We’re talking $50,000+ of spending per year. That’s not to say that spending $50,001 will get you Concierge Key status, but rather that if you spend less than that, don’t assume you have any real chance of being invited. As a matter of fact, nowadays you might need to spend significantly more than that. So you absolutely can earn Concierge Key purely through your own travel, and that’s probably the most common way it’s earned.

We don’t fully know what American looks for in this regard, though. Does the airline care purely about the dollar amount you spend, the typical fare classes you fly in (consistently full fare first class, for example), or something else? There are also some indications that the qualification criteria vary based on markets, so you have a better chance of earning it if you’re not living in a major hub city of American.

In other words, on some level it’s competitive, and you’re ranked against other travelers in similar markets. Expect that it takes more effort to earn Concierge Key if you primarily fly out of Charlotte (CLT), Dallas (DFW), or Miami (MIA), rather than out of Atlanta (ATL), Seattle (SEA), or Tampa (TPA).

Keep in mind that nowadays American Airlines elite status is based on the Loyalty Points program, so you can even earn elite status through credit card spending. So, does non-flying activity similarly count toward Concierge Key status? The reports I’ve seen suggest that it does, but you need to engage with the program a lot. For example, I’ve heard of people earning Concierge Key through credit card spending, but we’re talking about many hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending, if not over a million dollars.

You can also earn Concierge Key through the influence you have over others’ travel. Sometimes American Airlines will give Concierge Key nominations as part of a big corporate contract, or to key travel planners who have influence over a lot of others’ travel.

American Airlines is even known to comp Concierge Key to some “influencers.” For example, going back several years, YouTuber Casey Neistat was comped Concierge Key status and was really unhappy when it was taken away.

For avoidance of doubt, I’ve never been offered Concierge Key status, and I’m totally fine with that. 😉

Just for context on how these requirements compare to Executive Platinum, that requires 200,000 Loyalty Points per year. All AAdvantage members earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on credit cards, and Executive Platinum members earn 11x Loyalty Points per dollar spent on flights. So Executive Platinum requires $200,000 in credit card spending or around $18,200 in spending on flights.

American Concierge Key has quite a few published benefits, but some would argue the biggest benefit of the status is better “soft” treatment in the event of irregular operations.

The first thing worth understanding is that Concierge Key automatically comes with all Executive Platinum benefits. This includes everything from oneworld Emerald status, to space available first class upgrades, to complimentary Main Cabin Extra seating, to 120% bonus miles on flights, to three free checked bags, to a free drink & snack in economy, to priority services, to same day flight changes & standby.

This also includes access to the Loyalty Point Rewards program, allowing members to select additional perks, ranging from systemwide upgrades to bonus miles. Beyond that, benefits of American Concierge Key include the following:

Assistance during irregular operations is probably both potentially the most valuable perk, and also the most inconsistent one. On a good day, Concierge Key members may get proactive rebookings when flights are canceled and delayed.

American even has a fleet of cars at hubs for Concierge Key tarmac transfers, so during a short connection you may be picked up planeside and driven to your connecting flight. At the same time, there are also instances where you’ll likely be disappointed, because Concierge Key agents aren’t going to deliver 100% of the time.

If you’re looking to at least get Concierge Key levels of airport support with a particular trip, keep in mind that American offers Five Star Service, which is a paid program for more attentive service at the airport.

In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention some perks that Concierge Key used to offer, but no longer does:

American Airlines understandably hasn’t revealed how many Concierge Key members there are, so the best we can do is speculate. If I had to guess, I’d say there are somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 Concierge Key members. To be more exact, my assumption is that the number is roughly in the middle of that range.

In 2019 there was a clue — American worked with a company to send out chocolate to Concierge Key members, and the company posted that 11,300 packages had been prepared. Now, not all Concierge Key members received this chocolate, suggesting to me that there are more members than that.

If you’re curious how other elite ranks compare, I’d guess the number of Executive Platinum members is maybe 4-5x as high as the number of Concierge Key members. Again, that’s purely speculation on my part, and with the Loyalty Points system nowadays, the number may be even higher than that.

It’s hard to say whether something like Concierge Key is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Concierge Key varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Flagship Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal — you’ll get to board first, but there’s not necessarily all that much more to it.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including Delta 360 and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, though, I’d say that Concierge Key is probably the strongest of the tiers, in terms of the number of perks, including additional lounge access to the carrier’s most premium lounges. A couple of thoughts, though:

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. It gives you priority over Executive Platinum members for just about everything, lounge access, and also (hopefully) proactive help in the event of irregular operations. However, don’t expect it to earn it if you don’t spend at least $50,000 per year on American Airlines flights, and even then it’s not a sure bet.

Is the status life changing? While I’ve never had it, I’m inclined to say “no.” But others certainly may disagree…

If you’re a Concierge Key member (or have been one in the past), what has been your experience with the status? How does it compare to Executive Platinum status?

And you forgot to mention the super cool aircraft metal luggage tags (from retired AA Aircraft). Maybe minor for normal ppl but quite important for us AVgeeks

Always fascinating to read about CK. The staff at the FL in MIA seems to take great pride on their CK customers, a couple of times I overheard conversations between them telling how valuable their CKs are. @Lucky, isn't Flagship First Check-In also available at ORD? enjoyed it many times until 2025 with my non US OWE status

I would love to hear about someone’s experience as Ultimate Platinum with AF or GGL with BA. Although, it would be really interesting to know if anyone is a CK Diamond Plus member. Heard stories from a former CK Diamond about the amazing soft treatment so wonder how that stacks up to the Invitation Only tier.

I was a CK for 10 years thanks to my former employer (we did a lot of long haul international travel in business class). The automatic domestic upgrades were nice, the Flagship Lounge access impressed friends and family (said one experienced traveler when we were handed champagne at the FL in ORD, "Wow, I heard stories about this but assumed it was an urban legend"), the expediters at certain international airports were helpful, and getting to the front of the lines during storms and chaotic days like today was reassuring. The most important benefit, though, was the elimination of hassles -- the tight connection, the missed flight and, in one memorable case, helping my daughter get out of Paris in the midst of a nationwide transportation strike when she wasn't even flying AA. My colleagues and I referred to the CK team as "the angels" because they could perform miracles. We often joked (sort of) that our employer could cancel our health insurance, seize our retirement benefits, but that they would have to pry our CK card out of our cold, dead hands. When I left for a new position at a much smaller company, I was able to keep my CK status for the remainder of the program year (about six months). Watching it flip to "Executive Platinum" at 12:01 am on March 1 -- yes, I stayed up to mourn -- was unnerving, but somehow I survived...

#6144. New York Times Blames Trump For Air Safety Risks—Gets Blasted By The Independent NTSB

The National Transportation Safety Board says the New York Times distorted its comments to attack President Trump. The paper’s aviation safety story has bigger problems than just politics. It gets a major crash wrong and credits a pilot hours rule for a safety record that began years before the rule took effect. James Fallows’s “Is Air Travel Getting Less Safe?” describes real issues of overworked air traffic controllers, military aircraft operating around passenger flights, and safety recommendations that haven’t been adequately addressed. Then it tries to turn them into a story about Trump dismantling the institutions that keep us safe, even though the issues he cites have been going on far longer than the current administration. I’ve written predominantly critically about Trump since he first ran for president 11 years ago. I rejected his effort to blame diversity hiring for the American Airlines 5342 tragedy before investigators had established what happened. That doesn’t make every argument against him a good one. The Times introduces Fallows as an instrument-rated private pilot with more than 2,000 hours. That’s true but while he’s written extensively about aviation it’s an odd way to frame him as author of this story. He’s also Jimmy Carter’s former chief speechwriter, a longtime Atlantic writer and editor, and a familiar voice on NPR. His career has been about politics and public policy. His own introduction to the article frames the piece as meant to connect aviation under Trump with public health, international aid, diplomacy, higher education and the rule of law. Aviation is the vehicle for a larger political point. The piece isn’t really about aviation, it’s using aviation. The Independent NTSB Attacks The Piece The NTSB says the article: Distorts the agency’s responses with political statements intended to attack the current administration. Mischaracterizes the NTSB’s role in the 1,500 hour pilot requirement. Incorrectly implies negligence by the Black Hawk pilots involved in the Washington National Airport collision. The statement also thanks the administration for supporting the agency and providing resources. That last part is political messaging too. (Gratitude for a budget doesn’t answer address aviation safety, but is probably necessary as a defensive measure.) “We are disappointed that this article sensationalizes and politicizes tragedies.” The NTSB’s response to the New York Times Magazine. — NTSB Newsroom (@NTSB_Newsroom) November 12, 2026 Fallows interviewed NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy. The agency argues she’s being mischaracterized, but they don’t actually say how. In the article she says, “Recommendations alone don’t save lives. Action does.” Her own July statement about the Washington crash warned that delays implementing the board’s recommendations represented a continuing, unacceptable risk. The Article Gets The Colgan Air Crash Wrong Fallows spends considerable space describing the 2009 Colgan Air crash near Buffalo – as the last U.S. airline crash with loss of life before American 5342. In fact, PenAir flight 3296 overran the runway at Unalaska in October 2019, killing a passenger. His account has the Colgan Air plane accumulating ice until it becomes a “frigid brick.” He writes that by the time the captain recognized the problem, it “might already have become unflyable.” But that isn’t what the investigation found. The FAA’s accident analysis says icing wasn’t a cause. When the stall warning activated, the airplane wasn’t yet stalled. The captain pulled back on the controls and put it into a stall. The crew had failed to monitor their airspeed and mishandled the approach. And both Colgan pilots already had more than 1,500 hours: The captain had 3,379 hours. The captain had a history of training failures despite the hours. The first officer had 2,244 hours, including 1,470 hours as a light airplane flight instructor and 774 hours in turbine aircraft. The 1,500 Hour Rule For Co-Pilots Isn’t The Reason For The Safety Improvements After Colgan, Congress and regulators made several changes. Pilot rest rules improved. Training changed. Pilot qualification requirements changed. Sharing pilot records improved. Evidence that safety has performed well after a package of changes doesn’t establish that (1) every element of those changes (2) caused the improvements. And there’s strong reason to believe the the 1,500 hour rule has the opposite effect. It makes becoming a pilot take far longer and become far more costly, which keeps talented people from becoming pilots. Those with a higher opportunity cost, or lacking access to resources needed, get excluded from the pool of potential pilots. You’re then drawing from a smaller group. The NTSB didn’t recommend the 1,500 hour number. In 2010 Senate testimony, then-chair Deborah Hersman explained that the board had investigated accidents involving both high-time and low-time pilots. It found a relationship between failed practical tests and subsequent accidents, but there wasn’t evidence that number of hours actually mattered. The higher minimum took effect in 2013. Fallows’s safety streak begins in February 2009. The first four and a half years of that streak can’t be credited to a requirement that wasn’t yet in effect. Making pilots chase hours can allow relevant skills to deteriorate and bad habits to develop before an airline has to train those habits out of them. Repeated flights in clear weather, making takeoffs and landings at the same familiar airports, aren’t equivalent to structured training for instrument flying in a jet with another pilot, airline procedures, and complex air traffic control instructions. Hours in a hot air balloon count. The hot air balloon can be tethered. European co-pilots don’t face the same restriction, but their safety record is equivalent. Sub-1,500 hour European pilots fly in the United States every day without concern (and American pilots fly in Europe without elevated risk). The argument for the rule is that experience can build judgment, and that the higher threshold was part of a successful improvement in regional airline standards. But that’s an argument for useful experience and rigorous standards. That’s not what we got. An hour spent building time isn’t as valuable as an hour spent in a supervised airline training program. And there’s zero evidence that 1,500 is the right metric. It was chosen because it’s expensive and time-consuming, restricts entry into the pilot profession and drives up wages, and was supported by the major pilots union. The Black Hawk Crew Bears Responsibility The NTSB objected to Fallows implying negligence by the helicopter pilots. But its own probable cause finding identifies the helicopter crew’s failure to maintain effective visual separation as a cause of the collision. The crew accepted responsibility for avoiding the airliner and failed to do so. The existence of systemic failures don’t eliminate pilot error. In Homendy’s testimony explaining the findings, the board concluded that the helicopter’s altimeter probably understated its altitude by about 100 feet. The crew likely believed it was below the route’s ceiling. Fallows also describes the crew flying through civilian traffic without monitoring its traffic avoidance systems. The helicopter had no integrated cockpit traffic display. The pilots had tablets capable of showing traffic, but looking down at them while flying low at night with night vision goggles was problematic. Their audio alerts weren’t integrated into the pilots’ helmets. There were failures of FAA route design, and the FAA failed to act in the face of repeated warnings. But it’s genuinely weird to pin the blame for that on the first nine days of the Trump administration before the crash. I’ve criticized efforts to preserve military exceptions around Washington National. Civilian aviation shouldn’t have to accommodate unnecessary military risks. The Pentagon needs to change, and the current administration is responsible for making that happen. But it didn’t invent the culture that allowed these risks to exist in the first place. The Article’s Own Incident Data Doesn’t Support A Partisan Cause Fallows combines airline accidents, rocket debris, military encounters, airshow incidents and presidential flyovers which generally have different causes. And a list that attributes incidents while a given President is in office to that President doesn’t do a good job of evaluating what decisions caused those incidents. But more simply, even the article’s own figures for the most serious runway incursions are problematic for the Fallows narrative: 2023: 22 incidents. 2024: 7 incidents. 2025: 14 incidents. 2026 through October: 9 incidents. The increase from 2024 to 2025 looks dramatic – a doubling! But it’s still far lower than under Biden in 2023! These are relatively small numbers, and they don’t show a steadily worsening trend. (And there are more aircraft operations than in 2023.) Air Traffic Control Was Broken Before Trump Fallows points to deregulation and falling fares as sources of overcrowding. More people being able to afford to fly is a good thing, and flying is still safer than driving. The failure is an FAA air traffic organization system that hasn’t kept up with demand. The Times has done excellent reporting on this subject. In August 2023, I covered its investigation into 46 close calls in one month and roughly 300 near collisions in a year. Staffing shortages, fatigue, outdated equipment and a culture that tolerated recurring warnings weren’t the result of the 2024 election. Fallows discusses 132 union-represented FAA employees fired during the DOGE purge. Their union announced their reinstatement in March 2025. Firing them was disruptive, but he leaves out the reversal. And recruiting gamers doesn’t establish that the FAA is lowering controller standards. The FAA has been growing the top of the funnel but there’s no indication that unqualified people are being advanced in training to a greater degree. I’ve criticized Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for counting initial trainee hires as progress, that strikes me as juking the stats but hasn’t been a safety issue. And the Trump administration is doing modernization work that’s valuable and that’s been ignored for decades even if I’m skeptical that it’s close to enough because they don’t seem to be addressing the management problems at the FAA that created failed technology investment and decades-long controller shortages in the first place. I’ve been critical of pouring money into the existing organization. We need to address how air traffic control is managed, how it buys equipment, how it finances long projects and how it’s held accountable for performance. We’d be far better off separating the air traffic control operator from its regulator, with stable funding and professional management, as Canada has done with its nonprofit provider. His account has the Colgan Air plane accumulating ice until it becomes a “frigid brick.” He writes that by the time the captain recognized the problem, it “might already have become unflyable.” But that isn’t what the investigation found. The FAA’s accident analysis says icing wasn’t a cause. When the stall warning activated, the airplane wasn’t yet stalled. The captain pulled back on the controls and put it into a stall. The crew had failed to monitor their airspeed and mishandled the approach. And both Colgan pilots already had more than 1,500 hours: The captain had 3,379 hours. The captain had a history of training failures despite the hours. The first officer had 2,244 hours, including 1,470 hours as a light airplane flight instructor and 774 hours in turbine aircraft. The 1,500 Hour Rule For Co-Pilots Isn’t The Reason For The Safety Improvements After Colgan, Congress and regulators made several changes. Pilot rest rules improved. Training changed. Pilot qualification requirements changed. Sharing pilot records improved. Evidence that safety has performed well after a package of changes doesn’t establish that (1) every element of those changes (2) caused the improvements. And there’s strong reason to believe the the 1,500 hour rule has the opposite effect. It makes becoming a pilot take far longer and become far more costly, which keeps talented people from becoming pilots. Those with a higher opportunity cost, or lacking access to resources needed, get excluded from the pool of potential pilots. You’re then drawing from a smaller group. The NTSB didn’t recommend the 1,500 hour number. In 2010 Senate testimony, then-chair Deborah Hersman explained that the board had investigated accidents involving both high-time and low-time pilots. It found a relationship between failed practical tests and subsequent accidents, but there wasn’t evidence that number of hours actually mattered. The higher minimum took effect in 2013. Fallows’s safety streak begins in February 2009. The first four and a half years of that streak can’t be credited to a requirement that wasn’t yet in effect. Making pilots chase hours can allow relevant skills to deteriorate and bad habits to develop before an airline has to train those habits out of them. Repeated flights in clear weather, making takeoffs and landings at the same familiar airports, aren’t equivalent to structured training for instrument flying in a jet with another pilot, airline procedures, and complex air traffic control instructions. Hours in a hot air balloon count. The hot air balloon can be tethered. European co-pilots don’t face the same restriction, but their safety record is equivalent. Sub-1,500 hour European pilots fly in the United States every day without concern (and American pilots fly in Europe without elevated risk). The argument for the rule is that experience can build judgment, and that the higher threshold was part of a successful improvement in regional airline standards. But that’s an argument for useful experience and rigorous standards. That’s not what we got. An hour spent building time isn’t as valuable as an hour spent in a supervised airline training program. And there’s zero evidence that 1,500 is the right metric. It was chosen because it’s expensive and time-consuming, restricts entry into the pilot profession and drives up wages, and was supported by the major pilots union. The Black Hawk Crew Bears Responsibility The NTSB objected to Fallows implying negligence by the helicopter pilots. But its own probable cause finding identifies the helicopter crew’s failure to maintain effective visual separation as a cause of the collision. The crew accepted responsibility for avoiding the airliner and failed to do so. The existence of systemic failures don’t eliminate pilot error. In Homendy’s testimony explaining the findings, the board concluded that the helicopter’s altimeter probably understated its altitude by about 100 feet. The crew likely believed it was below the route’s ceiling. Fallows also describes the crew flying through civilian traffic without monitoring its traffic avoidance systems. The helicopter had no integrated cockpit traffic display. The pilots had tablets capable of showing traffic, but looking down at them while flying low at night with night vision goggles was problematic. Their audio alerts weren’t integrated into the pilots’ helmets. There were failures of FAA route design, and the FAA failed to act in the face of repeated warnings. But it’s genuinely weird to pin the blame for that on the first nine days of the Trump administration before the crash. I’ve criticized efforts to preserve military exceptions around Washington National. Civilian aviation shouldn’t have to accommodate unnecessary military risks. The Pentagon needs to change, and the current administration is responsible for making that happen. But it didn’t invent the culture that allowed these risks to exist in the first place. The Article’s Own Incident Data Doesn’t Support A Partisan Cause Fallows combines airline accidents, rocket debris, military encounters, airshow incidents and presidential flyovers which generally have different causes. And a list that attributes incidents while a given President is in office to that President doesn’t do a good job of evaluating what decisions caused those incidents. But more simply, even the article’s own figures for the most serious runway incursions are problematic for the Fallows narrative: 2023: 22 incidents. 2024: 7 incidents. 2025: 14 incidents. 2026 through October: 9 incidents. The increase from 2024 to 2025 looks dramatic – a doubling! But it’s still far lower than under Biden in 2023! These are relatively small numbers, and they don’t show a steadily worsening trend. (And there are more aircraft operations than in 2023.) Air Traffic Control Was Broken Before Trump Fallows points to deregulation and falling fares as sources of overcrowding. More people being able to afford to fly is a good thing, and flying is still safer than driving. The failure is an FAA air traffic organization system that hasn’t kept up with demand. The Times has done excellent reporting on this subject. In August 2023, I covered its investigation into 46 close calls in one month and roughly 300 near collisions in a year. Staffing shortages, fatigue, outdated equipment and a culture that tolerated recurring warnings weren’t the result of the 2024 election. Fallows discusses 132 union-represented FAA employees fired during the DOGE purge. Their union announced their reinstatement in March 2025. Firing them was disruptive, but he leaves out the reversal. And recruiting gamers doesn’t establish that the FAA is lowering controller standards. The FAA has been growing the top of the funnel but there’s no indication that unqualified people are being advanced in training to a greater degree. I’ve criticized Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for counting initial trainee hires as progress, that strikes me as juking the stats but hasn’t been a safety issue. And the Trump administration is doing modernization work that’s valuable and that’s been ignored for decades even if I’m skeptical that it’s close to enough because they don’t seem to be addressing the management problems at the FAA that created failed technology investment and decades-long controller shortages in the first place. I’ve been critical of pouring money into the existing organization. We need to address how air traffic control is managed, how it buys equipment, how it finances long projects and how it’s held accountable for performance. We’d be far better off separating the air traffic control operator from its regulator, with stable funding and professional management, as Canada has done with its nonprofit provider. The statement also thanks the administration for supporting the agency and providing resources. That last part is political messaging too. (Gratitude for a budget doesn’t answer address aviation safety, but is probably necessary as a defensive measure.)

“We are disappointed that this article sensationalizes and politicizes tragedies.” The NTSB’s response to the New York Times Magazine. — NTSB Newsroom (@NTSB_Newsroom) November 12, 2026

Fallows interviewed NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy. The agency argues she’s being mischaracterized, but they don’t actually say how. In the article she says, “Recommendations alone don’t save lives. Action does.” Her own July statement about the Washington crash warned that delays implementing the board’s recommendations represented a continuing, unacceptable risk.

(HT: Paddle Your Own Kanoo) Topics on this pageAviation safetyDonald TrumpJames FallowsNational Transportation Safety BoardThe New York TimesAir traffic controlAmerican AirlinesBuffaloCanadaColgan AirColgan Air Flight 3407Federal Aviation AdministrationJimmy CarterJoe BidenNational Public RadioRonald Reagan Washington National AirportSean DuffyThe TimesUnited States CongressUnited States Senate+15 more More From View from the Wing

The NTSB objected to Fallows implying negligence by the helicopter pilots. But its own probable cause finding identifies the helicopter crew’s failure to maintain effective visual separation as a cause of the collision. The crew accepted responsibility for avoiding the airliner and failed to do so. The existence of systemic failures don’t eliminate pilot error.

In Homendy’s testimony explaining the findings, the board concluded that the helicopter’s altimeter probably understated its altitude by about 100 feet. The crew likely believed it was below the route’s ceiling.

Fallows also describes the crew flying through civilian traffic without monitoring its traffic avoidance systems. The helicopter had no integrated cockpit traffic display. The pilots had tablets capable of showing traffic, but looking down at them while flying low at night with night vision goggles was problematic. Their audio alerts weren’t integrated into the pilots’ helmets.

There were failures of FAA route design, and the FAA failed to act in the face of repeated warnings. But it’s genuinely weird to pin the blame for that on the first nine days of the Trump administration before the crash.

I’ve criticized efforts to preserve military exceptions around Washington National. Civilian aviation shouldn’t have to accommodate unnecessary military risks. The Pentagon needs to change, and the current administration is responsible for making that happen. But it didn’t invent the culture that allowed these risks to exist in the first place.

Fallows combines airline accidents, rocket debris, military encounters, airshow incidents and presidential flyovers which generally have different causes. And a list that attributes incidents while a given President is in office to that President doesn’t do a good job of evaluating what decisions caused those incidents. But more simply, even the article’s own figures for the most serious runway incursions are problematic for the Fallows narrative: 2023: 22 incidents. 2024: 7 incidents. 2025: 14 incidents. 2026 through October: 9 incidents. The increase from 2024 to 2025 looks dramatic – a doubling! But it’s still far lower than under Biden in 2023! These are relatively small numbers, and they don’t show a steadily worsening trend. (And there are more aircraft operations than in 2023.) Air Traffic Control Was Broken Before Trump Fallows points to deregulation and falling fares as sources of overcrowding. More people being able to afford to fly is a good thing, and flying is still safer than driving. The failure is an FAA air traffic organization system that hasn’t kept up with demand. The Times has done excellent reporting on this subject. In August 2023, I covered its investigation into 46 close calls in one month and roughly 300 near collisions in a year. Staffing shortages, fatigue, outdated equipment and a culture that tolerated recurring warnings weren’t the result of the 2024 election. Fallows discusses 132 union-represented FAA employees fired during the DOGE purge. Their union announced their reinstatement in March 2025. Firing them was disruptive, but he leaves out the reversal. And recruiting gamers doesn’t establish that the FAA is lowering controller standards. The FAA has been growing the top of the funnel but there’s no indication that unqualified people are being advanced in training to a greater degree. I’ve criticized Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for counting initial trainee hires as progress, that strikes me as juking the stats but hasn’t been a safety issue. And the Trump administration is doing modernization work that’s valuable and that’s been ignored for decades even if I’m skeptical that it’s close to enough because they don’t seem to be addressing the management problems at the FAA that created failed technology investment and decades-long controller shortages in the first place. I’ve been critical of pouring money into the existing organization. We need to address how air traffic control is managed, how it buys equipment, how it finances long projects and how it’s held accountable for performance. We’d be far better off separating the air traffic control operator from its regulator, with stable funding and professional management, as Canada has done with its nonprofit provider. Fallows points to deregulation and falling fares as sources of overcrowding. More people being able to afford to fly is a good thing, and flying is still safer than driving. The failure is an FAA air traffic organization system that hasn’t kept up with demand.

The Times has done excellent reporting on this subject. In August 2023, I covered its investigation into 46 close calls in one month and roughly 300 near collisions in a year. Staffing shortages, fatigue, outdated equipment and a culture that tolerated recurring warnings weren’t the result of the 2024 election.

Fallows discusses 132 union-represented FAA employees fired during the DOGE purge. Their union announced their reinstatement in March 2025. Firing them was disruptive, but he leaves out the reversal.

And recruiting gamers doesn’t establish that the FAA is lowering controller standards. The FAA has been growing the top of the funnel but there’s no indication that unqualified people are being advanced in training to a greater degree. I’ve criticized Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for counting initial trainee hires as progress, that strikes me as juking the stats but hasn’t been a safety issue.

And the Trump administration is doing modernization work that’s valuable and that’s been ignored for decades even if I’m skeptical that it’s close to enough because they don’t seem to be addressing the management problems at the FAA that created failed technology investment and decades-long controller shortages in the first place.

I’ve been critical of pouring money into the existing organization. We need to address how air traffic control is managed, how it buys equipment, how it finances long projects and how it’s held accountable for performance. We’d be far better off separating the air traffic control operator from its regulator, with stable funding and professional management, as Canada has done with its nonprofit provider.

#6142. Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there. Understandably a lot of people get cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) to maximize the rewards they’re earning for their spending, and that’s a great idea. These cards offer valuable bonus categories, no foreign transaction fees, great travel coverage, and more.

But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense. That’s because hotel credit cards largely offer some incredible perks that more than justify the annual fee, including free hotel elite status, and even some free night certificates. So even if you’re not loyal to a hotel group, it’s easy to get outsized value.

In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.

There are hotel credit cards issued by Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, and World of Hyatt, which offer the opportunity to earn free night awards. To be clear, I’m not talking about the ability to earn points, but instead, the ability to earn free night awards that can be redeemed at a set of properties.

These free nights come in different forms — some free night awards are offered for spending a certain amount on a card, and some free night awards are offered as an annual benefit just for having a card, with no spending required.

So let’s take a look at the details of how these free night awards work, and then we’ll talk about whether they’re worth it. Note that I’m focusing specifically on cards that offer free night awards on an ongoing basis (rather than as part of a welcome offer), and am also limiting this to cards that are open to new applicants.

Hilton Honors has two credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Hilton Honors free night awards are my single favorite hotel free night awards out there, given that they have no category caps, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Hilton points at 0.5 cents each.

Hilton free night awards can be redeemed for standard rooms at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, and there’s only a small list of excluded properties. They’re even valid at Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties that are part of the Hilton Honors partnership. It’s easy to redeem these at properties costing $1,000+ per night.

IHG One Rewards has three credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

IHG One Rewards free night awards are also potentially quite valuable, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value IHG points at 0.5 cents each.

While IHG free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, what I really like is how you can top them off with an unlimited number of points. So if a hotel requires 100,000 points, you could use a 60,000 point free night certificate, and then top it off with 40,000 points.

Marriott Bonvoy has four credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Marriott Bonvoy free night awards are also extremely lucrative, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Marriott points at 0.7 cents each.

While Marriott free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, you can top them each off with up to 25,000 points, to redeem at more expensive properties. So you could book a hotel costing 60,000 points per night by redeeming a 35,000 point free night award, and then redeeming 25,000 additional points.

World of Hyatt Honors has one credit card that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

World of Hyatt free night awards are valuable, but definitely the most restrictive of the bunch. Free night awards issued with the card expire 12 months after they’re issued. I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

Category 1-4 covers a lot of Hyatt properties (these can cost up to 25,000 points per night), but the catch is that you can’t use these certificates to redeem at more expensive properties by topping them off. Still, it should be very easy to get outsized value.

I’ll let my credit card portfolio speak for itself — I have quite the selection of hotel credit cards. They’re not necessarily cards that I spend a ton on, but instead, they’re cards I largely have because of the very strong perks that they offer, which to me, more than justify the annual fee. Let me just give a few direct examples…

I have the Hilton Honors Aspire Card, and it’s my single favorite hotel credit card. The card offers a massive number of perks, but in particular, the free night alone more than justifies the annual fee for me. I try to use this at properties that would retail for $1,000+ per night, so it’s pretty awesome to get that, along with all kinds of other perks, just for having the card.

I also think there’s merit to spending $60,000 per year on the card, if you can swing it. That spending would earn you a minimum of 180,000 points (since you earn at least 3x points per dollar spent with the card), plus two additional free night awards, potentially worth up to 500,000 points. So this is a great card to consider if you’re making a big purchase.

In the case of Marriott Bonvoy, I have both the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card and Marriott Bonvoy Business Card, which get me free night awards worth 85,000 and 35,000 points, respectively. These also in and of themselves more than justify the annual fees on the cards. I generally redeem the larger free night award for a luxury hotel stay, while I redeem the lesser free night award for a stay at a mid-range property.

Lastly, I also have the World of Hyatt Credit Card, and that free night award also more than justifies the annual fee in and of itself. Admittedly I wish the free night award cap would be increased to reflect inflation, but even so, I get a ton of value out of this. At an absolute minimum, I use it when I have an overnight near JFK to stay at the Hyatt Regency JFK, which typically costs $300+ if paying cash.

There are potentially lots of great benefits to hotel credit cards, including big welcome bonuses, easy opportunities to earn hotel status, generous rewards structures for spending, and more.

The best part is that most issuers let you have multiple credit cards, meaning you can potentially earn more than one free night certificate per year. In the case of just about all of the above cards, I’d say the free night certificates more than justify the annual fees.

What’s your favorite hotel credit card free night certificate?

#6141. Here's How Boeing Killed 2 Birds With 1 Stone When It Built The 767's Gear Unlike Any Other Jet

The Boeing 767 is unique among Boeing aircraft for its main landing gear sporting a 'toe-down' (or forward tilting) position. The front wheels make contact with the runway before the rear wheels within the main landing gear assembly. In Boeing parlance, the orientation is referred to as the 'truck positioner' (or truck tilt actuator), while in Airbus' terminology it's referred to as the 'bogie pitch trimmer.'

The toe-down position is one of the easiest ways to visually identify a landing Boeing 767 from other Boeing widebodies, although not so much from Airbus aircraft, as some models have a similar configuration. Both Boeing and Airbus have switched the origination of the main landing gear within aircraft families depending on the requirements of the variant. Here is what to know about why Boeing designed the 767 (mostly) with toe-down landing gear and how that fits in with the wider industry.

The Boeing 767 has an unusual feature noted in the aviation community. It was designed with a conventional tricycle landing gear layout with a steerable twin-wheel nose gear and two four-wheel main landing gear bogies. When the 767 is airborne, its main landing gear bogies tilt forward in a toe-down position rather than the more conventional backward (toe-up) position. This is unique among Boeing aircraft.

The Boeing 767 comes in several variants: the 767-200, the 767-2C (KC-46A), the 767-200ER, the 767-300, the 767-300ER, the 767-300F, and the 767-400ER. Boeing developed the 767-400ER in the 1990s as a stretched aircraft for a limited lineup of airlines. The -400ER was the first Boeing widebody aircraft that resulted from two fuselage stretches.

The variant was ultimately unpopular, with only 37 examples being ordered by the two US-based airlines (Delta Air Lines and Continental), plus one testbed eventually delivered to Bahrain as a VIP transport. Boeing likely lost money on the program, although it never published the financial figures for it. The notable feature of the variant for this article is that Boeing replaced the standard 767 landing gear with taller, heavier 777-derived landing gear. This required a redesigned structure and deeper fairing. Consequently, the -400ER is the only 767 variant with standard backward tilting landing gear.

The 767 has a narrower cross-section than other widebodies like the 747 or Airbus A300, being designed as a mid-sized airplane for seven-abreast seating (2-3-2). The novel design is often credited with solving multiple issues. One benefit often seen mentioned by pilots and mechanics on aviation forums is that the configuration allows the gear to fit into a smaller wheel well. Some describe it as a "tight fit" and the best use of limited space.

The design avoids the need for large, drag-inducing blisters on the aircraft's belly. Another benefit was the Tilt Actuator Mechanism and how the aircraft lands. The tilt changes the aircraft's touchdown. The front wheels of each bogie make contact with the runway first, with the bogie then rotating level and the rear wheels settling. Some commentators say this helps to cushion the landing by spreading out the load more gradually and reducing stress on the landing gear.

Toe-up main landing gear (aft/rear wheels lower)

747 (wing gear only), 767-400ER (777-derived gear), 777, 777X, 787

The design comes with a de-rotation tendency, naturally pitching the nose slightly downward toward the runway on contact. This requires pilots to hold back pressure carefully during the flare in order to avoid a firm nose-gear slap. The advantages of the toe-up design were not enough for Boeing to retain it with other aircraft. It has not used the design for subsequent aircraft like the Boeing 777, 767-400ER, and 787.

The classic Boeing widebody is still going strong.

Almost all narrowbody airliners come with a single set of main landing gear wheels. Here, the Boeing 757 stands out due to being a large narrowbody designed to fill the mid-sized airplane gap. It is often categorized as a heavy narrowbody, sitting at the upper weight limit of narrowbodies—up to 255,000 lbs (115.6 t) MTOW on later models. Boeing's plans to develop the replacement New Mid-Sized Airplane, often called the 797, have not materialized.

The Boeing 757's bogies tilt slightly toe-down during flight. This means that the Boeing 767 is, strictly speaking, not unique among Boeing aircraft, but it remains more noticeable. The 757's bogies are slightly toe-down at around 5° to 8°, which is just enough to align the truck with the narrow fuselage wheel well during retraction. By comparison, the Boeing 767's angle is typically around 15°–17°.

It can also be noted that the Boeing 757 is closely related to the Boeing 767 widebody. It is useful to think of the Boeing 757 and 767 as fraternal twins developed in the late 1970s. They were designed to allow aircraft to enjoy interchangeability and minimal pilot training between types. The 757 has long been a favored aircraft on thinner transatlantic routes, although it is now being replaced by the A321neo.

The Boeing 767 has been an excellent airliner, with Boeing selling around 1,380 examples. Over time, its comparatively robust and heavy design that has made it particularly useful as a freighter compared with modern composite material aircraft. However, this also gave it an economic disadvantage as a commercial passenger airliner, and Boeing replaced it with the cleansheet Boeing 787 Dreamliner. That composite-heavy aircraft offers around 25% better fuel efficiency.

However, the Dreamliner did not replace the 767 as a freighter with the 787. Boeing continued to offer the 767, and companies continued to order it. In the end, it was stricter regulations that made the 767-300F infeasible as a freighter. The program is currently in the process of winding down (more below). The last of these freighters may continue flying into the 2050s or 2060s.

The passenger 767 fleet is approaching the end of its passenger career with airlines having phased out earlier models and leading operators (e.g., Delta, United, JAL, ANA) phasing them out and/or ordering their replacements. Delta withdrew three 767-300ERs in 2025 and another one so far in 2026, with the remaining -300ERs to be divested by 2030. Japan Airlines plans to retire and replace its fleet with the A321neo by 2028.

Dissecting the undercarriage of two revolutionary jetliners.

As of November 2026, Boeing has delivered 13 767-300Fs, leaving it with a remaining backlog of seven aircraft. Deliveries of the Boeing 767-300F freighter are fast coming to an end, although deliveries of the military Boeing 767-2C (KC-46A Pegasus) tanker are set to continue deep into the 2030s. The FAA provided an exemption from new emission restrictions for the Boeing 767-300F until 2033 under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024.

The FAA only has jurisdiction in the United States, with the regulations in force elsewhere in the world. Consequently, Boeing sought to deliver all its outstanding orders for the Boeing 767 in 2026 ( regulations enter into force on January 1, 2027). Boeing's 2026 records show it delivered the two outstanding 767-300Fs to FedEx in April and May and 11 of the remaining orders to UPS between February and October.

Now, Boeing's records only show seven remaining to be delivered to an 'unidentified customer'. These remaining orders appear to be for UPS (considered an open secret), with Boeing starting the year with eight units for unidentified customers, and that number is now seven. That aircraft apparently went to UPS. The order was placed in December 2024 and is likely to be the last set of commercial 767s to be delivered.

Toe-down main landing gear is much more common on Airbus aircraft. Airbus models with toe-down landing gear include the Airbus A350-900, the Airbus A380, and the A310. With the A350-900, the four-wheel bogies tilt toe-down by around 9.3° in flight, allowing them to align cleanly with the ceiling of the center fuselage bay. This was flipped on the stretched A350-1000. The -1000 features a six-wheel bogie and has a slight toe-up bias.

The A380 Superjumbo comes with a four-wheel wing gear bogie and six-wheel body gear bogies. Both of these bogies tilt down. The older A310 has a slight toe-down position on its main bogies, a departure from the mostly flat position on the earlier A300. Almost none of this conversation is relevant to the world's lineup of narrowbody aircraft, including the Boeing 737, Boeing 757, Airbus A320 family, A220, Embraer E-Jets, and Comac C919.

This is because these smaller aircraft use a single-axle, two-wheel main landing gear configuration. Put another way, there is nothing to tilt up or down. Exceptions are the Boeing 757 (mentioned above), some Tupolev airliners (e.g., Tu-154), a bizarre custom order of Indian Airlines A320s (1989 to early 1990s) with custom four-wheel main gear bogies, and early jetliners. All the early jetliners were retired as scheduled passenger aircraft.

#6139. Boeing Admits Its 737 Was Unsafe In Construction—Tells Door Plug Passengers Tough Luck On Punitive Damages

Boeing admits the 737 MAX 9 whose door plug blew out on Alaska Airlines flight 1282 “was not reasonably safe in construction” when it left the factory. But the planemaker is still fighting to keep passengers from collecting punitive damages. Its argument amounts to tough luck: the airplane was built in Washington, and Washington law generally doesn’t allow those damages. Boeing already won that argument against a mother and her son who was nearly sucked out of the opening in the fuselage. Another group of passengers is trying to show that the misconduct reaches back to decisions made at the company’s former Chicago headquarters – in order to access Illinois law. Boeing has formally acknowledged the defective construction that resulted in the blowout. On January 5, 2024, the Alaska Airlines jet was climbing out of Portland for Ontario, California when the plug departed the airplane at nearly 15,000 feet. The cabin rapidly depressurized. Oxygen masks dropped, belongings flew out, and the pilots brought the aircraft safely back to Portland. Spirit AeroSystems had built the fuselage. At Boeing’s Renton factory, the plug was opened for rivet repairs, then closed without reinstalling the four bolts that kept it from moving. I covered the whistleblower’s account of those missing bolts before investigators eventually confirmed them. The National Transportation Safety Board identified Boeing’s inadequate training, guidance and oversight as the probable cause. “Not reasonably safe in construction” is the language of Washington’s product liability law. A manufacturer can be strictly liable for injuries caused by a product that materially departed from its specifications when it left the manufacturer’s control. That leaves the fight to focus on the value of passenger injuries and whether Boeing can be punished beyond paying compensation. Last month, I wrote about Cynthia Tisher and her son, whose shirt was sucked off his body. According to their lawsuit, his seat pitched toward the opening. His mother held onto him, afraid he’d be pulled out, too. Other passengers helped them move away. Their federal lawsuit sought punitive damages against Boeing and Spirit AeroSystems. The judge ruled that Washington law governed and threw that request out. The blowout happened over Oregon, but the manufacturing failure occurred in Washington. The judge refused to reconsider. The current admission comes in litigation by a 47 plaintiff group suing Boeing, Spirit AeroSystems and Alaska Airlines, which claims Boeing management promised safety improvements to regulators and the public while failing to deliver them. They say decisions at the former Chicago headquarters helped produce the failures that sent this airplane out without its bolts. Boeing’s admission makes sense as litigation strategy. Boeing can argue testimony over how badly it acted is unnecessary to decide how much compensation each passenger deserves. And its strategy turns on getting punitive damages thrown out. Topics on this pageAlaska Airlines Flight 1282BoeingBoeing 737 MAXProduct liabilityPunitive damagesAlaska AirlinesCaliforniaChicagoIllinoisNational Transportation Safety BoardOntarioOregonPortlandRentonSpirit AeroSystemsWashington+11 more More From View from the Wing

Its argument amounts to tough luck: the airplane was built in Washington, and Washington law generally doesn’t allow those damages. Boeing already won that argument against a mother and her son who was nearly sucked out of the opening in the fuselage. Another group of passengers is trying to show that the misconduct reaches back to decisions made at the company’s former Chicago headquarters – in order to access Illinois law.

Boeing has formally acknowledged the defective construction that resulted in the blowout. On January 5, 2024, the Alaska Airlines jet was climbing out of Portland for Ontario, California when the plug departed the airplane at nearly 15,000 feet. The cabin rapidly depressurized. Oxygen masks dropped, belongings flew out, and the pilots brought the aircraft safely back to Portland.

Spirit AeroSystems had built the fuselage. At Boeing’s Renton factory, the plug was opened for rivet repairs, then closed without reinstalling the four bolts that kept it from moving. I covered the whistleblower’s account of those missing bolts before investigators eventually confirmed them. The National Transportation Safety Board identified Boeing’s inadequate training, guidance and oversight as the probable cause.

“Not reasonably safe in construction” is the language of Washington’s product liability law. A manufacturer can be strictly liable for injuries caused by a product that materially departed from its specifications when it left the manufacturer’s control. That leaves the fight to focus on the value of passenger injuries and whether Boeing can be punished beyond paying compensation.

Last month, I wrote about Cynthia Tisher and her son, whose shirt was sucked off his body. According to their lawsuit, his seat pitched toward the opening. His mother held onto him, afraid he’d be pulled out, too. Other passengers helped them move away.

Their federal lawsuit sought punitive damages against Boeing and Spirit AeroSystems. The judge ruled that Washington law governed and threw that request out. The blowout happened over Oregon, but the manufacturing failure occurred in Washington. The judge refused to reconsider.

The current admission comes in litigation by a 47 plaintiff group suing Boeing, Spirit AeroSystems and Alaska Airlines, which claims Boeing management promised safety improvements to regulators and the public while failing to deliver them. They say decisions at the former Chicago headquarters helped produce the failures that sent this airplane out without its bolts.

Boeing’s admission makes sense as litigation strategy. Boeing can argue testimony over how badly it acted is unnecessary to decide how much compensation each passenger deserves. And its strategy turns on getting punitive damages thrown out.

For those who are wondering why the article mentioned Washington law when the blow out occurred over Oregon, look up the Erie case. #6138. What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges. When I rank the lounges that I like the most, some readers understandably have very different takes.

I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.

Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.

Broadly speaking, what I’m looking for in a lounge is a (relatively) quiet place to sit, connect to Wi-Fi, recharge electronics, use a clean bathroom, and maybe have some water or coffee. Other things are good to have, but not something I necessarily expect.

There are also some deal killers for me when it comes to airport lounges. Personally, if a lounge is packed, I have no interest in being there, and that largely reflects that over the years, terminals have become much better places to spend time:

I figured I’d share my expectations for lounges, and I’ll break it up into three tiers of lounges (admittedly some of the lines are blurred here):

I think it’s also important to note that everyone is looking for different things in lounges:

I think the two below videos from Cathay Pacific from several years ago oh-so-beautifully sum up what makes lounges great. The commentary in the videos is almost poetic.

With that out of the way, let me share my basic expectations of various types of lounges, and admittedly these reflect my preferences and biases.

My expectations for Priority Pass lounges, airport contract lounges, airline membership lounges, and credit card lounges, are pretty simple. I’m happy if I can actually consistently get in and have a quiet place to sit. Sadly that’s not as straightforward as it may sound, with so many stories of lounges denying entry to club members, Priority Pass members, etc.

What sets a “basic” lounge apart? I’d say showers, bathrooms that are significantly nicer than in the terminals, workstations, a good food selection (ideally with hot food), good coffee, and employees who actually make you feel welcome.

Just to give some examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be exceptional:

My expectations are a bit higher for purpose-built international business class lounges. In addition to what I expect from the more “standard” lounges above, I hope that international business class lounges will have hot food, a more premium drink selection, showers, and workstations.

What sets an international business class lounge apart? I’d say a la carte dining, nap rooms, barista-made coffee drinks, and generally elevated decor.

Just to give a few examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be quite good (we’re actually pretty lucky in North America):

International first class lounges are as premium as they get, so expectations should be high. In international first class lounges I expect a la carte dining, barista-made coffee, some sort of an area to rest, a truly tranquil environment, and staff who make you feel welcome.

What sets an international first class lounge apart? Dining that’s (high-end) restaurant quality, an amazing drink selection, individual nap rooms, spa treatments, and a ground experience that extends beyond the lounge. That’s to say either tarmac transfers or an escort to the gate, and that’s no doubt an area where many airlines fall short.

I’ve reviewed the world’s top first class lounges in detail, so it’s no secret what my favorite options are the Air France La Premiere Lounge Paris and Lufthansa First Class Terminal Frankfurt.

We’re all looking for different things from airport lounges, and I think that’s totally fair. Standards should differ based on what kind of a flight you’re taking, how you access the lounge, what you’re trying to accomplish by visiting a lounge, etc.

Everyone will have a different take on which lounges are great vs. just okay, and that’s fine. While I care about tranquility and good coffee, others care about great food and drinks.

I’m curious to hear from OMAAT readers — what makes a lounge great, in your book?

#6137. Bitter Christmas: A Bah Humbug to Moviemaking

Almodóvar’s loss of creativity and camp is cause for alarm.

Pedro Almodóvar’s Bitter Christmas explores his own recent creative crisis. Using a prismatic structure, Almodóvar tells three stories that reflect one another with diminishing returns. These interwoven tales never blend due to the blockage suffered by gay male Spanish filmmaker Raul (Leonardo Sbaraglia, styled with a storm of gray-white hair to resemble Almodóvar himself). Viewers must do a meta reading about the nature and purpose of filmmaking and artistic expression.

Almodóvar makes the mistake of introducing Raul’s imaginary stories before revealing their real-life source. As Bitter Christmas becomes more and more convoluted and uninvolving, it undeniably reflects a peculiar Millennial crisis: the internalized post-Covid repression that has paralyzed many filmmakers. Once the most exciting filmmaker of the late 1980s, Almodóvar now suffers the same malaise that has also befallen comparable colleagues Martin Scorsese and Steven Spielberg. You don’t have to be a cinephile to realize that most contemporary filmmakers are bereft of fresh ideas and genuine inspiration.

Before getting to that core Raul/Almodóvar narrative, Bitter Christmas first presents stories in which a female filmmaker Elsa (Bárbara Lennie) imagines the drama of a woman, Patrizia (Victoria Luengo), who feels her same maladies and longs to escape an unhappy marriage, and then another woman, Natalia (Milena Smit), who is deep in mourning. This narrative contraption is the worst example of a gay male’s feminine empathy that Almodóvar has ever contrived. Unlike Law of Desire and Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown, this film lacks the camp buoyancy that made Almodóvar a comic hybrid of Jean Cocteau and Luis Buñuel, putting him at the vanguard of the world’s evolving sexual sophistication.

Now foregrounding his identification with female experience, Almodóvar seems to cater to political correctness rather than flout it. That a once-major pop artist can no longer make irresistible movies but instead succumbs to patronizing political trends is a cause for alarm more significant than any particular misbegotten film.

In one subplot, Raul is told, “You can lie in your life but not in your fiction,” referring to how he mistreats his partner Santi (Quim Gutiérrez) while also exploiting his assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón) as fodder for his newest script.

This contorted set-up suggests that Almodóvar feels pressure to join the global progressivism that a former bad boy of the Spanish underground is now obliged to endorse. That’s why the ultra-bourgeois Bitter Christmas lacks comedy and eroticism. Raul’s sex life is transferred to the shallow, quasi-porn of Elsa’s relationship with boytoy Bonifacio (Patrick Criado), a firefighter and part-time stripper (probably an homage to the superior João Pedro Rodrigues satire Will-O’-the-Wisp.

Almodóvar has lost audacity. Sadness pervades the movie. Its title comes from “Amarga Navidad” (“Bitter Christmas”), a ranchera (folk torch song) performed by Chavela Vargas. But this is the least impassioned film Almodóvar has made; its emotions are distanced by artifice — in imagination, storytelling, and performance. The projection of Raul/Almodóvar’s true feelings into fakery distances real life so much that the melodrama is drab. It’s not fabulous or funny (despite ornamental design and another urgent Alberto Iglesias score), but arid like Lanzarote, the black-sand volcanic island where make-believe characters Elsa and Victoria retreat into a dull version of Ingmar Bergman’s Persona — another go at Almodóvar’s insipid The Room Next Door. None of these meta-antics result in moral summation like Fellini’s masterpieces La Dolce Vita and Otto e mezzo.

Although Almodóvar avoids obvious political pronouncement like those that ruined Killers of the Flower Moon, West Side Story, and Disclosure Day, the twisted autobiographical aspects of Bitter Christmas still indicate that he suffers a similar personal liberal panic. (Unlike Spielberg and Scorsese, Almodóvar has made foolish partisan comments on American politics.) Almodóvar can’t escape the private anxiety that Scorsese and Spielberg experience along with the rest of us. Almodóvar’s inability to disentangle primal emotional need from political confusion is evident on screen in Bitter Christmas and ultimately unsatisfying.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

#6136. American Airlines Tells Flight Attendants To “Speak Up”—So Nearby Passengers Hear The Credit Card Pitch

American Airlines is teaching flight attendants to answer credit card questions loudly enough that nearby passengers hear the pitch, and to use stories about family, friends and other cardmembers to sell the benefits. A slide from recent flight attendant sales training lays out six tips. The most revealing one is “Speak up.” When one passenger asks about the card, American wants the answer to attract the attention of everyone around them. You may have declined the brochure, but the next row’s question is another chance to sell you. The slide presents these as best practices from fellow flight attendants: Share specific examples or stories. Use anecdotes from cardmembers, family or friends to explain how the card can help. Know your facts. Review the brochure and become comfortable discussing the benefits. Speak up. Answer questions at a volume that lets neighboring passengers hear. The slide says projecting your voice will attract their interest and curiosity. Take initiative. Coordinate with the other flight attendants about who makes the announcement and who walks the aisle. The cabin lights must remain on. Consider the timing of the flight and avoid making the announcement when the lights are off. Treat customer information confidentially. Never share, copy, photograph or retain personal information encountered on an application or screen. Knowing the product and protecting personal information are basic requirements. Coordinating the crew’s efforts means one announcement and brochures for passengers who want them. The stories, volume and lights are where this gets interesting. American Has More Riding On Its Citi Partnership Onboard credit card sales have been around for years. Under American’s old arrangement, Barclays had the inflight acquisition channel while Citi had other ways to acquire customers. The expanded Citi agreement brings those channels together under an exclusive U.S. card issuer. I’ve reported that the new relationship has been described to me as a joint venture. American’s stake goes beyond supplying miles and benefits to a bank. They’re more closely tied to the performance of the card business itself. A bank collects interchange, annual fees and interest, and pays for funding, credit losses, rewards and acquiring customers. Sharing in the economics of that business gives American more reason to care about who applies, who keeps the card, and who actually uses it. Getting another application on a flight is the beginning of that relationship. American also needs passengers to like the airline enough to keep it in their wallets. The sales push has been building. In May, I covered top inflight card sellers receiving a Clearwater, Florida getaway. Card approvals have also become accelerators in American’s flight attendant performance scoring. In August, I wrote about the push to get flight attendants more excited about selling. American was emphasizing both how much crew could earn and how providing better service would make passengers more receptive. The airline has a good audience for its card: people already buying its flights. Scott Kirby brought onboard pitches to United, which made them mandatory in 2018. These pitches work. Whether making them longer, louder or more frequent works well enough to justify annoying everyone else is a different calculation. Flight Attendants Object To Being Required To Train For Voluntary Sales On October 15, the Association of Professional Flight Attendants objected to American putting a 15-minute card sales module into mandatory fourth quarter training. According to the union, management first tried to include it in third quarter training, backed off after objections, then inserted it in the fourth quarter package. Completing the module qualifies flight attendants for the program and makes them eligible for a $25 qualification reward. Selling remains voluntary. The union’s objection is that employees who haven’t chosen to sell are being required to take the sales training anyway, and that required training should focus on safety, security and performing their jobs. Some flight attendants welcome commissions on approved applications. Others resent being drawn into selling financial products. Read The Script, Tell Stories, And Make Sure Other Rows Hear American’s announcement guidance requires the approved script to be read verbatim. It should take about a minute and be delivered once per flight segment. That’s in tension with telling flight attendants to share cardmember stories. Adding an anecdote to the announcement would depart from the script. And then there’s the direction to speak loudly enough that neighboring passengers hear. An individual conversation becomes an unscripted sales pitch to several rows. I’ve criticized onboard claims about bonuses covering two roundtrips to Hawaii when that wasn’t generally realistic. “Know your facts” is good advice. But familiarity with a brochure doesn’t necessarily equip someone to explain award availability or the restrictions on a benefit. Encouraging personal stories, delivered so that other passengers overhear, brings regulatory risk into the sales process. Lights On Shouldn’t Become A Reason To Keep Passengers Awake The slide says, “The cabin lights must remain on,” followed by an instruction to consider flight timing and avoid announcements when the lights are off. Read together, that means choosing an already illuminated part of the flight. It doesn’t tell flight attendants to turn on the lights and wake everyone for a pitch. American’s separate guidance says to make the announcement at cruise, before descent, between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. It excludes late night and redeye flights and tells crew to refrain during delays, diversions and other disruptions. Having the lights on doesn’t erase those restrictions. I covered similar limits in 2019, when American told me they were existing training rather than new rules. A slide from recent flight attendant sales training lays out six tips. The most revealing one is “Speak up.” When one passenger asks about the card, American wants the answer to attract the attention of everyone around them. You may have declined the brochure, but the next row’s question is another chance to sell you.

The slide presents these as best practices from fellow flight attendants:

Knowing the product and protecting personal information are basic requirements. Coordinating the crew’s efforts means one announcement and brochures for passengers who want them. The stories, volume and lights are where this gets interesting.

Onboard credit card sales have been around for years. Under American’s old arrangement, Barclays had the inflight acquisition channel while Citi had other ways to acquire customers. The expanded Citi agreement brings those channels together under an exclusive U.S. card issuer. I’ve reported that the new relationship has been described to me as a joint venture. American’s stake goes beyond supplying miles and benefits to a bank. They’re more closely tied to the performance of the card business itself. A bank collects interchange, annual fees and interest, and pays for funding, credit losses, rewards and acquiring customers. Sharing in the economics of that business gives American more reason to care about who applies, who keeps the card, and who actually uses it. Getting another application on a flight is the beginning of that relationship. American also needs passengers to like the airline enough to keep it in their wallets. The sales push has been building. In May, I covered top inflight card sellers receiving a Clearwater, Florida getaway. Card approvals have also become accelerators in American’s flight attendant performance scoring. In August, I wrote about the push to get flight attendants more excited about selling. American was emphasizing both how much crew could earn and how providing better service would make passengers more receptive. The airline has a good audience for its card: people already buying its flights. Scott Kirby brought onboard pitches to United, which made them mandatory in 2018. These pitches work. Whether making them longer, louder or more frequent works well enough to justify annoying everyone else is a different calculation.
