One of the most annoying moments on a flight is the credit card pitch over the loudspeaker, being forced to hear the 1,000th monotonous message. The airplane environment is already stressful enough from noise and crowding. It even pieces through my noise-canceling headphones.

Crews should not have to do this. They don’t want to. We, the passengers, don’t want them to. This is just management and banks forcing unnecessary things on all of us. Block spam.

This is just another reason I hate unions.

The last American flight I took was later October out of Phoenix. I don’t remember where the crew was based, but we were not subjected to the credit card spiel. I was going to thank them when disembarking but then thought that could cause problems for them. The lack of the sales push was enjoyable.

They don’t “have” to do it. Numerous other jobs don’t have this requirement. Update that resume.

To strengthen branding and passenger participation for the Citi®/AAdvantage® Executive card, I recommend putting the American Airlines and Citi logos on every sheet of aircraft lavatory toilet paper. Because nothing says “premium travel experience” quite like a captive audience using premium two-ply corporate messaging.

Of course crews should have to do this. The credit cards are the profit center of the airlines. You can’t complain about things like AA’s profitability on the one hand and then not play a role in pitching the profit center on the other.

And – spoiler alert – this is why having screens at every seat is essential. You can put your phone down for 30-60 seconds when the wifi ads play. But screens that cannot be turned off that are directly in front of your face…

What you really want is a 45 second celebrity video pitching the card first, and then the FAs come back over the loudspeaker with the current offer and then walk down the aisle smiling with the applications.

And gamify it! Everyone can apply while they are in flight with free wifi. First one on the plane that applies gets an extra 10k miles on top of the already generous SUB. Second person gets an extra 5k. Something like that.

It’s only a matter of time before FAs that sell the most get to jump up the seniority ladder. I’d be pushing for that hard if I was negotiating the next union contract on the airline side.

@Peter — The excessive and needless financialization of everything is leading us to another totally avoidable 1929, lest we forget. Airlines do not need to be credit cards with wings (and many around the world simply are not).

@Johnny — The flight attendants unions don’t want any of this; they represent their members who don’t either.

@Mike P — Take down your silly Civil Peace flag, Ayn Rand.

From the merger of an airline that at one point, couldn’t give us a beverage without opening an advert for the card (that would be the tray table), or god forbid, let us walk through the middle of any corridor at PHL without tripping over about 10 carts hawking the card…

“The excessive and needless financialization of everything is leading us to another totally avoidable 1929,…”

“Take down your silly Civil Peace flag, Ayn Rand.” He can’t refute the argument, so he resorts to a mindless insult. Typical

I fly a lot. I have yet to see a single person take interest in credit cards being hawked or even ask a question.

Get over it people. David says he has never seen someone take an application. LOL. Many FAs for AA make over 2k per month in sales commissions. (Verified) 24k extra salary per year for doing something voluntary and momentarily is nothing to sneeze about. The 15 minute training is great as it gives the hardest workers more I kwowledge to make more money.

@1990 – I mean, that’s a bit of a leap. Ads are pervasive in our society. You want to go see a movie – you’re going to see some ads before that movie, including for other movies. You want to watch a sporting event? Ads, ads, ads. Riding on the subway? Ads everywhere – including on video ad screens. The idea that we should have some cultural expectation that an airline tube is some “sacred space” where folks can’t be subjected to an ad for 1-2 minutes… I don’t buy it.

Flight attendants are the fire safety not for marketing nor salesman.. terrible that the company exposed them to do sales like a market.. unacceptable…

@Peter — Bit of a false equivalency, but I’m not saying ‘no advertising at all,’ just saying, the crew shouldn’t need to do this; before free WiFi? On the screen? SkyMall? Ok, I get those. Why AA does this but Delta and United doesn’t (or at least not as overtly, lately.)

@Mike P — I expected you to say, “I do not recognize your jurisdiction.” Regardless, doubling-down on your strawmen doesn’t make them real… I accept your surrender.

I would like to see data on how many card applications are submitted on board.

@1990 – why shouldn’t the crew have to do this? One may wish the profit center of the airline was elsewhere, but the idea that employees should not even try to contribute to the profit center of the airline seems anathema to me. I realize that the crew is of course primarily there for safety reasons, but this is literally an extra 2 minutes of work, during a time that they are getting paid to work. It’s ok to pass out drinks but not sign up bonuses? It’s ok to sell buy on board cheese plates but not credit cards? Why?

Now, one can make a judgment as to whether their performance should be evaluated on pitching a credit card. Lots of factors as to why someone might sign up for a card. But in an over-saturated market, having more ‘touches’ with respect to a product helps to sell that product. And companies, in general, are in the business of making money, and therefore want to promote their products. And FAs are, you know, representatives of their company.

Personally I’m shocked that the airlines have not tried to better monetize the FAs they have working for them that do YouTube/tiktok or whatever on the side. You’d think those FAs would naturally want to pitch cards for their respective airlines.

I’ve always felt that if the credit card pitches were more bespoke, perhaps they would get more sign-ups?

the old catch 22 game that AA plays.. participating in the program is considered “voluntary” but the flight attendants are required to take the training, and thus ” registered” to promote the cards.. now what can AAL do? well, you took the training , you are registered so when we tell you you HAVE to promote the card, WE can fire you for NOT promoting it.. win for the company.. not so much for the crew.. and regrettably the Union won’t do much about it.. sure they’ll make some token noise, but in the end, they’ll give in.

@ Peter…so, next time you go to a “quality” restaurant ( not a fast food joint) you won’t mind if the wait staff start running advertising speeches at you while you eat, of course the Valet will pitch you while you wait for the car, and when they arrive with the bill you’ll get just one more sales pitch.. ah the joy of an evening out.

#6135. Hilton Honors Amex Card Bonus: Points + Free Night Award Welcome Offers

For applications through January 13, 2027, American Express and Hilton are offering increased welcome offers on their four co-branded credit cards, and these are among the best deals we’ve seen on the cards. With these lucrative welcome offers, you can earn both points and an uncapped free night award (valid at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, which is Hilton’s highest award cost for standard room redemptions).

Not only are these great welcome offers, but these cards offer valuable benefits for those who stay at Hiltons with any frequency, so if you travel often, it’s worth having (at least) one of these cards in your wallet. In particular, I love the free night awards, given that they can even be redeemed at top Waldorf Astoria or Conrad hotels, or even Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties.

Link: Learn more about the Hilton Honors American Express Card, Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card, Hilton Honors American Express Business Card, and Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card

For applications through January 13, 2027, Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards are offering limited time welcome offers, which are among the best that we’ve ever seen on these cards.

In addition to offering bonus points, three of the cards also include a free night award as part of the bonus (and the fourth card offers a free night award as an annual benefit, including the first year). For the purposes of framing the value of the points, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each.

These are standard Hilton Honors free night awards, which can be redeemed at a vast majority of Hilton Honors properties around the world for a standard room, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I’d consider this to be the single most valuable hotel credit card free night award out there, given that it can be redeemed at a property costing up to 250,000 points per night.

Let’s go over the details of the Hilton card bonuses, from least premium to most premium. First, below is a quick chart comparing the Hilton Honors Amex welcome offers (let me emphasize that the welcome offer value doesn’t factor in the free night awards, which arguably make up a majority of the value with these offers).

The Hilton Honors American Express Card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees), and for applications through January 13, 2027, the card has a limited time welcome offer of 70,000 Hilton Honors bonus points plus a free night award after spending $2,000 within the first six months.

Beyond the welcome offer, the Hilton Honors Amex Card features the following perks in the long run:

Read a full review of the Hilton Honors Amex Card.

The Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card has a $150 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and for applications through January 13, 2027, the card has a limited time welcome offer of 130,000 Hilton Honors bonus points plus a free night award after spending $3,000 within the first six months.

Beyond the welcome offer, the Hilton Honors Surpass Card features the following ongoing benefits:

Read a full review of the Hilton Honors Surpass Card.

The Hilton Honors American Express Business Card has a $195 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and for applications through January 13, 2027, the card has a limited time welcome offer of 150,000 Hilton Honors bonus points plus a free night award after spending $8,000 within the first six months.

Beyond the welcome offer, the Hilton Honors Business Card features the following perks in the long run:

Read a full review of the Hilton Honors Business Card.

The Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card has a $550 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and for applications through January 13, 2027, the card has a limited time welcome offer of 200,000 Hilton Honors bonus points after spending $6,000 within the first six months.

While not explicitly being marketed as part of the welcome offer, keep in mind the card always offers a free night award on an annual basis, including the year in which you open the card. So for all practical purposes, think of the welcome offer as being 200,000 points plus a free night award.

Beyond the welcome offer, the Hilton Aspire Card features the following ongoing benefits:

Read a full review of the Hilton Aspire Card.

Anecdotally Hilton Honors Amex cards are pretty easy to be approved for:

If you’re trying to decide which of these offers makes the most sense, here are a few considerations:

For applications through January 13, 2027, Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards are offering limited time welcome offers. Three of the four cards are offering points plus a free night award, while the most premium card is offering a best-ever offer in terms of the number of points you can earn.

If you’re looking for a no annual fee card, then the Hilton Honors American Express Card is for you. Meanwhile, if you’re looking for a card with stronger perks and an even better bonus, I recommend the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card or Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card. The Hilton Honors American Express Business Card is also a good option for small businesses.

#6134. Virgin Atlantic Cancels 3 Long-Haul Routes: See Full List Now

Virgin Atlantic, like many other airlines, has been making several changes to its route network this year. Since March, the airline has completely withdrawn from the Middle East, and it recently confirmed that it will not resume flights between Manchester Airport (MAN) and Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) for summer 2027.

The decision comes as the SkyTeam member is basing a fifth aircraft at its Manchester hub next summer. It has also confirmed plans to increase frequencies on several existing routes as part of its summer 2027 schedule.

Since tensions in the Middle East escalated in late February, several airlines have temporarily paused or cut flights to the region. Virgin Atlantic was no exception. Before its withdrawal, the airline served two destinations in the region: Dubai International Airport (DXB) in the United Arab Emirates and King Khalid International Airport (RUH) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The latter was a relatively new addition to its network, having launched in March 2025.

The airline operated daily seasonal flights between London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and Dubai using its Airbus A350-1000 aircraft. Its Riyadh service, on the other hand, operated daily throughout the year using the Airbus A350-900. Initially, the UK airline announced that it was temporarily suspending both routes due to escalating tensions in the region. However, it subsequently decided to cancel them permanently.

According to data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, Virgin Atlantic's last scheduled flights to both destinations were in mid-March 2026, and no further services are currently scheduled. Separately, its London Heathrow–Tel Aviv route (which it last operated in 2023 when the conflict began) remains suspended, and flights are not expected to resume.

Furthermore, another notable change came recently when Virgin Atlantic confirmed that it would not return to Las Vegas from the Northwest England airport next summer. The airline first launched flights between the two cities in 2011 and continued operating the route until 2019. It then reinstated services in June 2024.

This year, the SkyTeam member operated the route between April and October and was scheduled to return on April 13, 2027, running through October 31. The airline had planned three weekly services, reducing to two during the peak summer months. However, these flights have now been canceled. Well, the route's performance may help explain the decision.

According to data from the US Department of Transportation (DOT), Virgin Atlantic filled just 72.3% of its seats between Manchester and Las Vegas in the 12 months to July 2026. This was around ten percentage points lower than its London Heathrow–Las Vegas route, where it operates daily year-round flights using a 258-seat Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner.

Instead of daily flights to Dubai, the airline will increase its capacity to South Africa, adding a new destination and increasing frequency.

The Las Vegas cancelation comes as Virgin Atlantic has announced plans to increase frequencies on its three remaining US routes from the airport. According to the airline's original schedule for July 2027, it had planned 24 weekly departures across these three routes. That number will now increase to 40.

Flights to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) will increase from daily to 11 weekly, while services to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) will rise from seven to up to ten weekly. Orlando International Airport (MCO) will see the largest increase, from 12 to up to 19 weekly flights.

That said, London Heathrow will continue to account for the majority of Virgin Atlantic's transatlantic capacity, representing roughly 84% of its transatlantic flying. The airline will continue to offer regular flights to 11 US destinations from the West London airport, including JFK, Boston, Atlanta, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Las Vegas, Miami, Orlando, Seattle, Tampa and Washington, DC.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6133. How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt. What are the best ways to redeem World of Hyatt points, how many points do you need for a free night redemption, how does the award chart work, etc.?

Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. There’s no science to that, but rather I think that’s a fair, conservative valuation for what the points are worth. In other words, I won’t redeem points for a hotel stay with Hyatt unless I’m getting well over 1.4 cents of value per point (and that has to factor in the points I’m forgoing by redeeming rather than paying cash, etc.).

It’s important to come up with a points valuation for yourself (it can be different than mine), so that you can decide whether to pay cash or redeem points for a hotel stay.

I have lowered this valuation a little recently, in light of the World of Hyatt award chart devaluation we’ve seen, where Hyatt has gone from three tiers of pricing within each category to five.

World of Hyatt has no blackout dates, which is to say that if a standard room is available for sale with cash, it can also be booked with points.

Now, the important thing to keep in mind is that some hotels have a very small pool of “standard” rooms, and a vast majority of rooms at a hotel may be considered “premium.” If a hotel has 150 rooms, it’s possible that only 10 rooms are considered “standard,” so that’s the major issue you’ll run into when redeeming points at some properties.

Unfortunately in the hotel industry overall, we’ve seen a reduction in the number of standard rooms at many properties that are popular for redemptions, which is essentially a way for hotels to create indirect capacity controls.

Keep in mind that Hyatt has a great points availability calendar, which at least makes it easy to find the nights that are available with points, for those properties that are challenging.

Hopefully this isn’t an issue anyone runs into, but just keep in mind the World of Hyatt points expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. Any points earning or redemption activity resets the expiration of your points by a further 24 months.

Unlike Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt continues to publish award charts for award redemptions (the exception is Mr & Mrs Smith properties, which I’ll talk more about in a bit).

The catch is that at this point, World of Hyatt has five tiers of award pricing for standard room redemptions — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper, and Top — and the variance within each category is huge. So while I appreciate that there’s not technically dynamic pricing, when a Category 1 hotel can cost 3,000 or 9,000 points, and a Category 8 hotel can cost 35,000 or 75,000 points, you’re not exactly getting a lot of assurance.

The standard award chart applies at a vast majority of properties globally, including most Hyatt branded properties. There are eight categories of hotels, and 40 different pricing tiers, given the five pricing bands within each tier. Pricing ranges from 3,000 points for a Category 1 property during the “Lowest” period, and 75,000 points for a Category 8 property during the “Top” period.

Next, World of Hyatt has an all-inclusive award chart, which applies to an ever-growing number of properties across Hyatt’s all-inclusive brands. Hotels fall into one of six categories, with the similar five bands of pricing, all based on double occupancy. Pricing ranges from 12,000 points for a Category A property during the “Lowest” period, to 85,000 points for a Category F property during the “Top” period.

Lastly, World of Hyatt has an award chart for Miraval properties, which are Hyatt’s super-luxurious wellness resorts. Pricing varies based on single or double occupancy, and then there’s also the five bands of pricing.

Note that unlike Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt doesn’t offer a fifth night free on award redemptions. So you’ll pay the points that correspond to the number of nights you’re staying.

World of Hyatt is the only major hotel loyalty program that lets you efficiently redeem your points for suites. This can come in the form of free night redemptions, or in the form of an upgrade award. Unlike with standard room availability, there are capacity controls on suite redemptions, so these won’t always be available just because a suite is for sale.

You can find the standard suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, the premium for a standard suite can range from around 20% to 100%, so there’s quite a bit of variance here. In many situations this could represent a good deal. Of course the ways that hotels choose to designate suites differs by property, so in some cases this can represent a huge upgrade, while in other cases it doesn’t.

You can find the premium suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, there’s also quite a bit of variance here in terms of how much of a premium you’re paying.

World of Hyatt also lets you upgrade to club rooms, suites, and premium suites, using points. You can find the chart for that below, though note that this is only possible when booking a fully paid stay at the flexible rate directly with Hyatt. This requires a rate code, so it’s not even combinable with Hyatt Privé rates.

There are also more capacity controls here than you’d have if redeeming Hyatt suite upgrade awards, which are issued through the Milestone Rewards program.

World of Hyatt offers Points + Cash awards, whereby you can book a stay at a hotel using a combination of points and cash. This might sound appealing to those who want to reduce the cash cost of a stay using points, or those who don’t have quite enough points for a stay.

Points + Cash redemptions follow an award chart. The way this works, you can redeem 50% of the standard points required, plus you’ll receive around 50% off the cash component of a stay, in comparison to the flexible rate.

It’s always worth taking a look at this, though more often than not I don’t find this to be as good of a deal as just outright redeeming points. Also note that Points + Cash redemptions have capacity controls, unlike free night redemptions.

Hyatt acquired luxury travel company Mr & Mrs Smith, and you’ll find that many Mr & Mrs Smith properties are bookable through Hyatt channels. This is an opportunity to earn and redeem Hyatt points for stays at all kinds of independent luxury properties that you’d not otherwise have access to with a major loyalty program.

While the opportunity to earn points is potentially exciting, the catch is that points redemptions largely represent a bad value. Award pricing is fully dynamic, and you’ll find that in many cases, points only get you around a cent each toward a stay. That’s significantly less than I value them, so I wouldn’t recommend redeeming that way.

While I wouldn’t say it’s my favorite use of points, World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, whereby you can redeem points toward a folio credit that can be applied to on-property dining and spa awards. With this, you’ll get anywhere from 1.0 to 1.54 cents of value per point.

While there are some restrictions to be aware of, this is still something that has the potential to be useful for those with lots of points, who are looking to splurge on incidentals during a stay.

With the Milestone Rewards program, World of Hyatt members can earn Guest of Honor certificates. This extends World of Hyatt Globalist status benefits over the course of a stay, for up to seven nights. These can be applied to any eligible revenue stay or points stay, and offer lots of value.

Those booked with a Guest of Honor certificate receive the standard Globalist perks, including complimentary breakfast, suite upgrades subject to availability, and much more. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there.

World of Hyatt has a generous policy when it comes to letting members transfer or combine points between accounts. World of Hyatt members can transfer points between accounts at a 1:1 ratio.

Members can transfer a minimum of 1,000 points, and can transfer in increments of 500 points above that. Members can transfer up to 525,000 points per transaction, and may transfer or receive up to that many points across accounts per calendar year. World of Hyatt accounts must be at least 60 days old in order to send or receive points.

World of Hyatt members are also limited to making one free points transfer every calendar month, and six free points transfers every calendar year. Transfers generally happen within 24 hours, but in rare cases could require additional review, and could take up to 10 business days.

This can be a great way to combine points in order to have enough for a particular redemption, or even to transfer points in order to make a booking out of an elite member’s account, or using a Guest of Honor award.

Nowadays many properties charge resort fees or destination fees, which are essentially a money-grab. All World of Hyatt members don’t have to pay these when redeeming points, which can add significant value. Furthermore, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay these even on revenue stays.

As a further perk, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay for parking on award stays (however, non-Globalist members do have to pay for parking).

World of Hyatt has three elite tiers — Discoverist (10 elite nights), Explorist (30 elite nights), and Globalist (60 elite nights). While status isn’t quite as easy to earn as with some other hotel groups, there are still some opportunities to earn status with credit cards. World of Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards include the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more). You can earn elite qualifying nights and status with these cards:

Even if you’re not a Hyatt loyalist, the great news is that earning World of Hyatt points is pretty easy. However, the ratios aren’t as consistently good as in the past.

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

On top of that, World of Hyatt frequently has promotions for purchasing points. The reason this matters is because there are lots of situations where you could get outsized value simply by buying points from Hyatt and then immediately redeeming them for a hotel stay.

With the above basics out of the way about redeeming World of Hyatt points, how do you get the most value with your points? Let me share my approach to redeeming Hyatt points.

As a Hyatt Globalist member, I exclusively redeem my points for free night award redemptions in standard rooms. While I think there can be value in redeeming points for standard or premium suites, my general strategy is to redeem for standard rooms, and then use suite upgrade awards to confirm suites.

The reality is that I get huge value with my World of Hyatt points throughout the award chart, and not just at aspirational properties. Generally I decide to redeem points if I’m getting at least two cents of value per World of Hyatt point. There are several things I factor into that, though. When deciding whether to redeem points:

With World of Hyatt charging such vastly different amounts across the five bands of pricing, in some cases you’ll get the most value per point when redeeming during an off-peak period, while in other cases you’ll get the most value when redeeming during a peak period. You of course always want to compare the cash rates to the points redemption rates.

With a little bit of effort, I have no issues redeeming a vast majority of my Hyatt points for well over two cents each, in comparison to the cash cost.

Ultimately the reason I collect airline miles and hotel points is for aspirational redemptions. I try to redeem for things that I typically wouldn’t pay for in cash, where I’m getting outsized value.

So just as airline miles are best redeemed for first & business class travel, hotel points are often best redeemed for five-star properties that would cost a lot in cash. So the main reason I earn Hyatt points is to be able to redeem at properties belonging to brands like Alila and Park Hyatt. From Alila Napa Valley, to Alila Ventana Big Sur, to Alila Jabal Akhdar, to Park Hyatt Kyoto, to Park Hyatt Milan, to Park Hyatt Paris, I’ve had some amazing award redemptions over the years.

World of Hyatt is my all-around favorite hotel loyalty program. I greatly value the elite perks I receive as a Globalist member, and I also consistently get great value with my points, especially for aspirational properties. I also love how World of Hyatt points can efficiently be transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, providing an easy pathway to racking up this currency.

Personally my favorite use of World of Hyatt points is for stays at Hyatt’s top luxury hotels, where you’ll almost consistently get the best value, assuming you can find award availability. However, I’ve gotten great value at lower end properties as well.

Now, in fairness, the value of Hyatt points is definitely decreasing a bit at the moment, and on top of that, the reduced transfer ratio from other currencies is frustrating, and definitely eats into the value a bit. That being said, that’s true of the industry at large, as we’ve also seen endless devaluations with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy. I do still get the most value with Hyatt.

What has your experience been with redeeming World of Hyatt points?

At the end of the day, when you factor in the time, effort and frustration, you end up losing more than you gain. #6131. Why Your Airline Credit Card Is Worth Keeping—But Rarely Useful For Spending

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

An airline credit card can save you enough in checked bag fees to justify keeping it, but cost you hundreds of dollars in rewards if you use it for your spending.

In this week’s episode of Airlines Confidential, Ed Pizzarello favored flexible bank points while former American AAdvantage President Maya Leibman preferred the simplicity of airline and hotel cards. Later, she recalled something an unnamed former loyalty program president had told her:

“people will pay anything for a free flight.”

For at least the last decade and a half I’ve been arguing that getting an airline card for benefits doesn’t mean it should become your default payment method, and that there are different distinct reasons to get a card besides payment processing (and bundled financing): An initial bonus. Spending enough to earn a large bonus can make sense even when the card’s normal earning rate isn’t attractive. And the bonus can be a reason to apply for the card, but you still need to decide if it’s worth using for ongoing spend. Benefits that come with keeping it. Checked bags, boarding benefits, lounge access or an anniversary certificate can justify the annual fee. The card may belong in the sock drawer, not your wallet, if actual rewards for spend aren’t great enough. Rewards for actual spending. This is where the return on the next dollar matters, including any status credit or spending threshold you’re working towards. Some benefits require paying with the card. Make the purchases needed to use those benefits. That still doesn’t make the card the best choice for the rest of your spending. Holding a UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees) is great if you fly United because you earn more miles, and then you spend fewer miles on your redemptions. That doesn’t require spending on the card itself. What Your Free Flight Actually Costs Put $30,000 of spending on a card earning one airline mile per dollar, and you earn 30,000 miles. Put the same spending on a 2% cash back card and you earn $600. You wouldn’t pay 2 cents per mile to buy miles, but that’s what you’re doing at 1 mile per dollar of spend, leaving aside other benefits from that spending (such as credit towards airline status). If you use those 30,000 miles for a flight you could have bought for $300. You’ve given up $600 to avoid paying $300. That’s just dumb. If the same miles buy a trip you’d actually pay $900 for (not just one that’s priced at $900 but where you’re unlikely to spend that), it’s anothe matter. That’s why airline miles make more sense for premium cabin international awards than domestic coach ones – because there’s generally more leverage when redeeming the points. And if the spending also earns credit towards status or another useful benefit, it can make sense also. Scott McCartney compared cash back with the value of individual hotel points and airline miles. But you have to multiply the value of each point by how many you earn. A half-cent point earned twice per dollar is a 1% return. The same point earned six times per dollar is 3%. You Can Earn Airline Miles Without An Airline Card Leibman’s preference for simplicity is fine as far as it goes, but bank points don’t require abandoning airline awards. You can keep points flexible – such as on a Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) or a Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees) – and transfer them when you find the award you want. Even American, which was long unusually difficult to access through transferable bank points, is now a Citi transfer partner. The same bank sells you American’s credit card and a competing currency that can become American miles or points in other programs. Spend on a Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) or a Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) and transfer to AAdvantage. That flexibility lets you choose where to redeem instead of committing all your earnings before you know which program has the best deal. American’s cards earn Loyalty Points towards status and it’s uncapped. And, as I recently explained about the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard®, eligible employee-card spending can earn status credit for both the employee and the primary cardmember at the same time. That’s a reason I’d consider moving spending: earning status for my wife as well as myself. If the same miles buy a trip you’d actually pay $900 for (not just one that’s priced at $900 but where you’re unlikely to spend that), it’s anothe matter. That’s why airline miles make more sense for premium cabin international awards than domestic coach ones – because there’s generally more leverage when redeeming the points. And if the spending also earns credit towards status or another useful benefit, it can make sense also. Scott McCartney compared cash back with the value of individual hotel points and airline miles. But you have to multiply the value of each point by how many you earn. A half-cent point earned twice per dollar is a 1% return. The same point earned six times per dollar is 3%. You Can Earn Airline Miles Without An Airline Card Leibman’s preference for simplicity is fine as far as it goes, but bank points don’t require abandoning airline awards. You can keep points flexible – such as on a Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) or a Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees) – and transfer them when you find the award you want. Even American, which was long unusually difficult to access through transferable bank points, is now a Citi transfer partner. The same bank sells you American’s credit card and a competing currency that can become American miles or points in other programs. Spend on a Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) or a Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) and transfer to AAdvantage. That flexibility lets you choose where to redeem instead of committing all your earnings before you know which program has the best deal. American’s cards earn Loyalty Points towards status and it’s uncapped. And, as I recently explained about the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard®, eligible employee-card spending can earn status credit for both the employee and the primary cardmember at the same time. That’s a reason I’d consider moving spending: earning status for my wife as well as myself. #6130. How the Electoral College Dies

Blue-state activists are about to be perfectly positioned to execute an end run around the constitutional system.

In the wake of the 2026 midterms, we are on the cusp of a total transformation of the U.S. election system. After decades of Republican dominance in state legislatures, Democrats now control enough state governments to push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past its 270-vote activation threshold and dismantle the Electoral College from below.

But it seems like the right has barely realized the importance of the fight that’s about to begin.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

#6129. FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop, Shuts Down The Skies: What’s Going On?

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented. Admittedly we’ve had our fair share of air traffic control issues in the United States over the years. But this is really on a different level, unlike anything we’ve seen since 9/11, in terms of operational disruptions. I guess it’s fitting that this is happening on Friday the 13th.

At 3:54PM ET today (Friday, November 13, 2026), the FAA issued a ground stop for flights across the country, as pilots received the following message:

DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

As of now, the ground stop is through 11:30PM ET, though it’s possible that it’s lifted before then. That timeline clearly reflects the extent to which the current situation is a complete mess, and this won’t be an easy fix.

As usual, JonNYC was among the first to break the news, and he even reported on this before the official ground stop was issued, when airports in the Northeast started having issues, prior to this going nationwide.

Kind of major, started at approx 3:15pmBoston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center, New York Approach have all lost numerous frequencies. All facilities are in ATC Alert. Some sectors in New York Center are unable any traffic currently. Numerous— I mean NUMEROUS frequencies…

“All airspace is currently being sterilized and centers are preparing for ATC Zero operations. Airborne’s should NOT be majorly effected— i.e, at least for now, this is not a “9/11 type of event” where airbornes are being forced to land at the closest airport available. All…

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed this development a while later, sharing that there were “communication issues impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” and he stated that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

As of now, there’s no timeline for this ground stop ending. To my knowledge, I believe this is now the most significant ground stop we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years (since 9/11).

If you’re flying this weekend, expect that things will be a mess. To those flying right now, good luck. Ford is on a flight that was supposed to depart at 3:59PM, so suffice it to say that he had some pretty bad luck here, as they pushed back, and then this happened. I hope not too many others are in the same situation.

There’s a major issue when you have flights landing but flights can’t depart, since you have way more planes than gates. So get ready to be patient if you’re onboard a flight, given the complicated logistics.

What could explain an air traffic outage of this scale? As of now, all we can do is speculate, though there are a few interesting things to point out.

First, it remains to be seen if this is related, but the FAA reportedly began its rollout of the new AI-powered air traffic management tool this week, known as SMART (which stands for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories”).

Timing-wise, it seems like there’s a possibility this could be related. At the same time, you wouldn’t assume this leads to communication issues, which is what seems to be going on here. So it’s worth pointing out the timing, but we have no reason to believe the two things are related.

Yes the FAA began its nationwide rollout of the SMART AI for ARTCCs to use this week. It’s not clear at this time if the rollout is related to this outage, but if it’s a rolling communications issue, it’s much more likely it’s within already established equipment pilots-ATC use https://t.co/PXqSFdOA1q

One can’t help but wonder if a cyber attack might be to blame. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin insists that there are no indications of this being a cyber attack. However, if they’re still investigating the cause, it seems hard to rule anything out.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the agency had no indications of outages being tied to a cyberattack or potential terror threat, adding that the nationwide ground stop was “just a telecommunications outage." https://t.co/cb8xON9Xrz

If this is truly “just a telecommunications outage,” then that represents a major failure. How can air traffic control nationwide have that issue, rather than it just being isolated to one region? Are there no redundancies?

I don’t want to be a conspiracy theorist, but it sure feels to me like some very unusual things are going on. We just saw a huge Microsoft outage, and it has been a very strange week in general. Those two things can of course be completely unrelated, but you can’t help but point it out.

The FAA has grounded flights nationwide, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” For nearly two hours now, no flights have taken off in the United States, making this the largest outage since 9/11, to my knowledge.

It remains to be seen what the cause of this was, and whether this is a tech glitch, a cyber attack, or what. To those flying now (or this weekend), good luck… you’re going to need it!

What do you make of this strange ATC outage?

Not sure if I misheard, but they let slip in the press conference exactly what the issue is. They connected new equipment to the old legacy and overwhelmed it. This was clearly an IT screw up whilst trying to incrementally upgrade the infrastructure. No more complex than that..... Or somebody plugged a laptop into the network and tried to pre-load GTA6 :-)

#6128. Chase’s New $350 IHG Card Offers 200,000 Points—Plus $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (See rates and fees)

Chase’s new $350 annual fee IHG credit card can return $400 in flight credits before your first renewal, on top of a 200,000-point initial bonus. It also gives you enough elite nights to choose a confirmable suite upgrade without first earning those nights through hotel stays.

I covered the changes to Chase’s IHG card portfolio earlier, but the new IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card deserves a good look. I’ve generally thought of IHG cards as something to get for the bonus and keep for the benefits. This one gives me a reason to consider putting some spending on it, too.

And Chase confirmed to me that its elite nights stack with those from other IHG cards. For someone who already has both the Premier and Business cards, adding Premier Select means 50 annual elite nights total starting with the existing cards’ January 2027 deposits which is enough to choose hotel lounge membership without stays or spending.

The launch offer lets you earn 200,000 IHG points after $5,000 in purchases within three months of account opening. At my half-cent valuation, the 200,000-point bonus is worth $1,000. Having another IHG personal or business card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The published restriction applies to current holders of this particular card, and previous holders who received its new cardmember bonus offer within the past 24 months. Chase told me that 5/24 applies. How To Get $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal The card offers a $200 airline statement credit per calendar year through December 31, 2027. It takes a single purchase of at least $250 in flight tickets booked directly with an airline. Open the card this fall, make a qualifying purchase in 2026, and make another in 2027 before your first anniversary. That’s $400 back against airfare you’d otherwise buy, compared with a $350 first-year fee. The spending has to land in the appropriate calendar year, so I wouldn’t leave the December purchase until the last minute. That’s a particularly good first year deal. For ongoing value, one $200 airline credit leaves $150 of annual fee to justify. The currently published benefit ends in 2027, so we’ll see if it continues after that. But $150 should not be hard. The Free Night And Hotel Dining Benefits Additional key benefits include: A free night after each account anniversary, capped at 60,000 points. You can add your own points for a more expensive redemption. A 90,000-point night would take the certificate plus 30,000 points. The stay must be completed within 12 months of issuance. This starts at your first anniversary. Up to $300 a year in IHG Food & Beverage Rewards. You get one $75 voucher each quarter. It expires at the end of the quarter, must be applied to eligible charges on your room folio during a participating stay, and any unused balance disappears when you redeem it (e.g. use just $45 and you lose the other $30). Every fourth night free on qualifying points stays. This applies to consecutive standard room award nights at the same hotel. Certificates don’t substitute for the points nights needed to trigger it. Automatic Platinum status. That brings benefits including upgrades subject to availability, but it doesn’t include Diamond’s breakfast welcome amenity choice. Up to $50 in United TravelBank cash. Register to receive $25 in each half of the year. The first-half deposit expires July 15 and the second-half deposit expires January 15 of the following year. I wouldn’t value the dining vouchers at $300 unless I already expected eligible hotel dining in every quarter. And while a 60,000 point certificate can replace $300 worth of points at my valuation, it’s less flexible than 60,000 points in an account since you have to use it for one night before it expires. There are smaller benefits as well like an application fee credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or NEXUS; no foreign transaction fees; and a 30% points-purchase discount that doesn’t stack with other purchase promotions. There’s also a year of DoorDash DashPass and three months of Instacart+, with enrollment by December 31, 2027, plus monthly $10 non-restaurant DoorDash and $10 Instacart offers through that date while the relevant membership is active. A Suite Upgrade Choice Without 20 Hotel Nights The card comes with 20 elite night credits on opening and annually thereafter. Chase allows six to eight weeks for the initial credits, with subsequent annual deposits due by February 1. They count toward both elite status and Milestone Rewards. At the 20-night milestone you can choose 5,000 points, two $20 Food & Beverage Rewards, or one confirmable suite upgrade. I’d take the upgrade. That upgrade can cover an eligible stay of up to five nights, including a points stay. You call IHG between 14 days and 24 hours before arrival to confirm an available entry-level suite. It isn’t a promise that every hotel will have a suite for your dates, and the rules exclude free night certificates and certain brands and rates. The award expires 12 months after selection. At 40 nights you get two milestone choices, which can include both annual hotel lounge membership and another confirmable suite upgrade. The lounge membership covers the member and one guest on eligible stays at hotels with a participating lounge. It lasts through the end of the year you earn the milestone and the following calendar year. Elite Nights Stack Across Cards Chase confirmed to me: Cardmembers who hold multiple IHG One Rewards Credit Cards will receive the applicable Elite Night Credits each card provides. For existing cardmembers, annual ENCs will first be deposited in January 2027. New accounts opened on or after October 1, 2026, will receive their applicable ENCs upon card opening. In addition, cardmembers can earn 2 ENCs for every $5,000 spent on each eligible card, with spending tracked separately by card account. That corrects the non-stacking language many folks originally noted on the application page. For existing cardholders adding Premier Select, the January 2027 deposits mean: Premier Select plus either Premier or Business: 35 annual elite nights. That leaves just five qualifying hotel nights to reach the 40-night lounge-membership choice. Premier Select plus both Premier and Business: 50 annual elite nights. That gets you the 40-night choices, including lounge membership and a suite upgrade, plus the 50-night reward choice, without hotel stays or card spending. The timing is different for new accounts: cards opened on or after October 1 qualify for their opening credits now. Existing accounts receive their first annual deposits in January. And the spending counters stay separate—$3,000 on one card and $2,000 on another won’t combine into a $5,000 block that earns two nights. $15,000 In Spending Is More Interesting Than It First Looks The card earns 12 points per dollar at participating IHG hotels, 6 on dining and other travel, and 3 on other purchases. At half a cent per point, those are returns of 6%, 3% and 1.5%. Chase’s advertised “up to 28X” at IHG includes base hotel program earnings and the Platinum bonus not just the rewards for credit card spend. But there are spending rewards that change the calculation. You earn two elite nights per $5,000 in purchases, plus five additional nights and 20,000 bonus points at $15,000 in calendar-year spending. Here’s what the card alone produces, assuming the nights credit in the same calendar year. The spending thresholds are cumulative so actual qualifying hotel nights would add to these totals. Calendar-Year Spending   Total Card Elite Nights   Additional Spending Benefits Earned $0   20   20-night milestone choice $15,000   31: 20 + 6 + 5   20,000 bonus points; also reaches the 30-night milestone $25,000   35: 20 + 10 + 5   Diamond status through the following calendar year $40,000   41: 20 + 16 + 5   Additional free night capped at 60,000 points, with points top-up allowed; also reaches the 40-night milestone On $15,000 of purchases earning 3 points per dollar, you’d receive 45,000 points plus the 20,000-point spending bonus. That’s 65,000 points worth $325 at my valuation, compared with $300 from a 2% cash back card, before assigning anything to the eleven additional elite nights or the 30-night milestone choice. That’s better than just a basic return of just 3 points per dollar which I view as about 1.5%. At $40,000, you’d have 140,000 points from those same unbonused purchases and the spending bonus, worth $700 versus $800 in cash back. You’d also have Diamond status, the additional free night, and enough nights to select lounge membership and another suite upgrade. You earn two elite nights per $5,000 in purchases, plus five additional nights and 20,000 bonus points at $15,000 in calendar-year spending. Here’s what the card alone produces, assuming the nights credit in the same calendar year. The spending thresholds are cumulative so actual qualifying hotel nights would add to these totals. Calendar-Year Spending   Total Card Elite Nights   Additional Spending Benefits Earned $0   20   20-night milestone choice $15,000   31: 20 + 6 + 5   20,000 bonus points; also reaches the 30-night milestone $25,000   35: 20 + 10 + 5   Diamond status through the following calendar year $40,000   41: 20 + 16 + 5   Additional free night capped at 60,000 points, with points top-up allowed; also reaches the 40-night milestone On $15,000 of purchases earning 3 points per dollar, you’d receive 45,000 points plus the 20,000-point spending bonus. That’s 65,000 points worth $325 at my valuation, compared with $300 from a 2% cash back card, before assigning anything to the eleven additional elite nights or the 30-night milestone choice. That’s better than just a basic return of just 3 points per dollar which I view as about 1.5%. At $40,000, you’d have 140,000 points from those same unbonused purchases and the spending bonus, worth $700 versus $800 in cash back. You’d also have Diamond status, the additional free night, and enough nights to select lounge membership and another suite upgrade. The card offers a $200 airline statement credit per calendar year through December 31, 2027. It takes a single purchase of at least $250 in flight tickets booked directly with an airline.

Open the card this fall, make a qualifying purchase in 2026, and make another in 2027 before your first anniversary. That’s $400 back against airfare you’d otherwise buy, compared with a $350 first-year fee. The spending has to land in the appropriate calendar year, so I wouldn’t leave the December purchase until the last minute.

That’s a particularly good first year deal. For ongoing value, one $200 airline credit leaves $150 of annual fee to justify. The currently published benefit ends in 2027, so we’ll see if it continues after that. But $150 should not be hard.

Additional key benefits include: A free night after each account anniversary, capped at 60,000 points. You can add your own points for a more expensive redemption. A 90,000-point night would take the certificate plus 30,000 points. The stay must be completed within 12 months of issuance. This starts at your first anniversary. Up to $300 a year in IHG Food & Beverage Rewards. You get one $75 voucher each quarter. It expires at the end of the quarter, must be applied to eligible charges on your room folio during a participating stay, and any unused balance disappears when you redeem it (e.g. use just $45 and you lose the other $30). Every fourth night free on qualifying points stays. This applies to consecutive standard room award nights at the same hotel. Certificates don’t substitute for the points nights needed to trigger it. Automatic Platinum status. That brings benefits including upgrades subject to availability, but it doesn’t include Diamond’s breakfast welcome amenity choice. Up to $50 in United TravelBank cash. Register to receive $25 in each half of the year. The first-half deposit expires July 15 and the second-half deposit expires January 15 of the following year. I wouldn’t value the dining vouchers at $300 unless I already expected eligible hotel dining in every quarter. And while a 60,000 point certificate can replace $300 worth of points at my valuation, it’s less flexible than 60,000 points in an account since you have to use it for one night before it expires. There are smaller benefits as well like an application fee credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or NEXUS; no foreign transaction fees; and a 30% points-purchase discount that doesn’t stack with other purchase promotions. There’s also a year of DoorDash DashPass and three months of Instacart+, with enrollment by December 31, 2027, plus monthly $10 non-restaurant DoorDash and $10 Instacart offers through that date while the relevant membership is active. A Suite Upgrade Choice Without 20 Hotel Nights The card comes with 20 elite night credits on opening and annually thereafter. Chase allows six to eight weeks for the initial credits, with subsequent annual deposits due by February 1. They count toward both elite status and Milestone Rewards. At the 20-night milestone you can choose 5,000 points, two $20 Food & Beverage Rewards, or one confirmable suite upgrade. I’d take the upgrade. That upgrade can cover an eligible stay of up to five nights, including a points stay. You call IHG between 14 days and 24 hours before arrival to confirm an available entry-level suite. It isn’t a promise that every hotel will have a suite for your dates, and the rules exclude free night certificates and certain brands and rates. The award expires 12 months after selection. At 40 nights you get two milestone choices, which can include both annual hotel lounge membership and another confirmable suite upgrade. The lounge membership covers the member and one guest on eligible stays at hotels with a participating lounge. It lasts through the end of the year you earn the milestone and the following calendar year. Elite Nights Stack Across Cards Chase confirmed to me: Cardmembers who hold multiple IHG One Rewards Credit Cards will receive the applicable Elite Night Credits each card provides. For existing cardmembers, annual ENCs will first be deposited in January 2027. New accounts opened on or after October 1, 2026, will receive their applicable ENCs upon card opening. In addition, cardmembers can earn 2 ENCs for every $5,000 spent on each eligible card, with spending tracked separately by card account. That corrects the non-stacking language many folks originally noted on the application page. For existing cardholders adding Premier Select, the January 2027 deposits mean: Premier Select plus either Premier or Business: 35 annual elite nights. That leaves just five qualifying hotel nights to reach the 40-night lounge-membership choice. Premier Select plus both Premier and Business: 50 annual elite nights. That gets you the 40-night choices, including lounge membership and a suite upgrade, plus the 50-night reward choice, without hotel stays or card spending. ” It lasts through the end of the year you earn the milestone and the following calendar year.”

Some nuance here – the lounge membership lasts the year you redeem the award, which may be up to 90 days after “you earn the milestone”. #6127. Duffy And Mullin’s FAA Ground Stop Press Conference: Self-Praise, A $50 Billion Ask, And Conflicting Stories

Yesterday, we saw the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issue a nationwide ground stop, which wasn’t fully lifted for over four hours. This represents the single biggest grounding of flights in the United States since 9/11, so the scale of whatever happened is pretty wild.

At around 8PM last night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to update people on the state of things. I can’t help but cover this, because it felt like something between an SNL skit and a shakedown, and they couldn’t even keep their story straight… all while praising themselves for doing an unprecedented job!

Below you can find the press conference last night regarding the FAA shutdown, which happened around the time that the ground stop was lifted. First Mullin and Duffy spoke for around 10 minutes, and then they took questions for around 20 minutes.

The gist of the story is that they claim there were no signs of this being a cyber attack, and basically they broadly blame the outdated air traffic control system.

Mullin didn’t speak for long, and his primary comment was this:

“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like, by the organization and team he has put together. We are built to handle crises like this, and that’s exactly what we’re doing. We’re moving at an unprecedented pace, as a whole of government, to make sure we’re doing the public justice by making sure everyone is safe, which everyone is.”

Isn’t this a little self-congratulatory, especially while he’s also claiming that they don’t fully know the cause here? Just objectively, the pace was indeed unprecedented… it was the longest ground stop since 9/11!

Then you have Duffy speak, and this basically just turned into a demand for Congress to give him $50 billion to modernize our aviation infrastructure, while not actually being honest about the state of things:

“The President, for the last year, has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a new air traffic control system.”

That’s just not accurate at all. In July 2025, Congress authorized $12.5 billion for modernizing air traffic control, which Duffy described as a “down payment.” Since then, the size of the request kept changing, and the formal ask only went to Congress this week, when Duffy asked lawmakers for $30.1 billion for air traffic control and airport upgrades.

So it’s a bit rich to claim that Congress has been uncooperative over the past year, especially when you consider Republicans have controlled the White House, House, and Senate.

He then tried to explain what happened, which just feels like a complete deflection to me, as it’s about an overall need to modernize ATC, rather than what actually went wrong here:

“What happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down… I shouldn’t say they went down… they started to give us inconsistency with the data from those routers, and because of that, we shut the system down. Now, I have already replaced some of those switches with President Trump, and our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down, and I think the question for the American people is, ‘do you want your Congress to fund this?'”

“I think the Congress at a point looked at the history of the FAA, and said ‘we don’t trust you.’ Well with President Trump, and what we’ve done, I think they do trust, because what we’ve done with that first tranche of money.”

“I’ve asked the President to ask for $30 billion. I want $50 billion.”

Obviously our air traffic control technology is really outdated and does need updating, there are no two ways about it. However, what was different yesterday, and caused an outage to this scale?

You can see I quoted Duffy above as saying that he claimed that “what happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data,” and that this caused the shutdown. I’m not a tech expert, but how exactly does that happen and cause the systems nationwide to have issues? At most, you’d assume it would be regionalized, no?

So this is where the questions from reporters come in handy. Mullin seemingly threw Duffy under the bus, saying:

“What it appears to be right now is that as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches in the system, they were putting new equipment, and new technology, and that new equipment and new technology was overwhelming the older system.”

You can see Secretary Duffy’s reaction as Secretary Mullin says the newer technology was overwhelming the system. pic.twitter.com/IeoW5nM4aY

Duffy was then asked what was different yesterday, given that the system had been in place for years. As you’d expect, there was no good answer.

Initially Duffy made it sound like they knew exactly what happened, but then he backtracked on that, and said “we’re still working on the details of what went wrong, I’ll be happy to give you more information, but I don’t want to give you the wrong information.”

Very good set of questions from Luke Radel for Secretary Duffy and Secretary Mullin. pic.twitter.com/f6tlfDtbJG

I also appreciate how someone actually asked the question about this being blamed on Congress, given that the Republicans have had full control for the past two years. As you’d expect, Duffy’s response was first to ask what network the person was from.

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

What’s amazing to me is the overall tone of the press conference. They feel bad for themselves, with Duffy pointing out that he hopes he doesn’t have to give another press conference after 8PM. You know what’s not mentioned once, though? Thanking travelers for their patience throughout all of this, or apologizing to the public for the disruption. Not once.

I’m 100% in support of funding and modernizing air traffic control. But when you have the biggest outage you’ve had in over 25 years, it seems a bit rich to say “give us $50 billion” and “we’re doing an unprecedented job.” And again, if Mullin is to be believed, the system updates that were put in place were to blame.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference last night about the nationwide ground stop, and it just struck me as being incredibly tone deaf and off base.

#6126. How Much Wider Is The Boeing 787's Fuselage Compared To The 767?

Boeing built both the 767 and 787 to serve similar roles, albeit decades apart. Each is an example of a twin-engine widebody designed to serve medium- to long-haul routes, but at a fraction of the cost of more fuel-hungry quadjets. Naturally, the newer technology available when the 787 — or Dreamliner as it is known — was built means it trumps its older counterpart in efficiency and range.

But passenger comfort is another matter, and whether one aircraft offers a better experience for those on board than the other is somewhat debatable when it comes to the 767 and 787. No doubt, the 787 has the edge in several areas. Fuselage width, however, does not necessarily work in its favor, despite the 787 offering more space in this sense than the 767.

As to how much wider it is, the short answer is: Significantly enough. The 787’s fuselage measures an extra two feet, five inches (0.74 meters) in width than the 767’s. Internally, the distance between each cabin wall is a slightly more moderate two feet, four inches (0.71 meters) greater aboard the 787 than the 767. That applies to all variants within the respective 787 and 767 families, given that each set of aircraft shares a common cross-section.

Although the differences cited above may appear marginal, they do have very real ramifications for airlines and passengers alike. With an interior trim-to-trim width of 15 feet, six inches (4.72 meters), the 767 allows for rows of seven abreast economy seats laid out in a 2-3-2 configuration, according to Boeing aircraft characteristics documents. Each walkway running down the cabin is said to measure one foot, seven inches (0.48 meters) across.

Boeing 767 and 787 family fuselage cross-section widths:

In contrast, the 787’s internal cabin width of 18 feet (5.49 meters) means enough space is available for airlines to fit rows of nine economy seats in a 3-3-3 configuration. Its walkways also measure a slightly smaller one foot, six inches (0.46 meters) in the standard cabin, per the Boeing documents. All of that goes to say, the 787 does boast a wider fuselage and internal cabin, but that does not necessarily translate to more room per passenger onboard.

Beyond space per passenger, in economy seating at least, the 787 trumps the 767 on pretty much every other metric. Boeing officially launched the Dreamliner program in 2004, well after the 767’s own introduction. Come 2011, when the 787 debuted commercially with All Nippon Airways, the airliner was unlike anything that had come before it.

Instead of relying so heavily on traditional materials such as aluminum, Boeing primarily built the 787s out of carbon fiber composites. Such materials, which are lighter and more resistant to corrosion, make up roughly 50% of the aircraft by weight, according to the manufacturer. That means “less fuel to lift, cruise, climb and maneuver,” as Boeing writes. Coupled with improved aerodynamics and newer engine technology, that translates to a 25% reduction in fuel burn compared to the planes the 787 was intended to replace.

Boeing 787 family specifications, from Boeing:

GE Aerospace GEnx-1B / Rolls-Royce Trent 1000

GE Aerospace GEnx-1B / Rolls-Royce Trent 1000

GE Aerospace GEnx-1B / Rolls-Royce Trent 1000

But the wide use of composites in the 787 has offered benefits beyond just improved efficiency. For passengers, dehydration and jet lag are common effects of long-haul flights. Boeing was able to incorporate features into the 787 to mitigate both, though. Given that carbon composites do not rust, cabin humidity levels can be kept higher in the newer-generation widebody. Similarly, fatigue-resistant properties allow a lower cabin altitude—which plays a large part in the severity of jet lag—to be maintained than on older aluminum aircraft.

The Dreamliner achieves its fuel efficiency and range flexibility through advanced materials, aerodynamics, and smart design.

In contrast, the 767 is very much a product of its time. Developed alongside the Boeing 757, the 767 program was officially launched back in 1978. The widebody then made its first commercial flight with United Airlines in 1982. Needless to say, technology moved on a fair bit in the near-three-decade gap between the 767 and 787’s respective entries into service.

As with many aging models built primarily from aluminum, the 767’s cabin altitude tends to sit in the 7,000- to 8,000-feet (2,137 to 2,439-meter) range. That is cut to 6,000 feet (1,829 meters) on the 787, meaning passengers experience a smaller drop in blood oxygen saturation—which itself contributes to classic jet-lag symptoms. Humidity in the 767 and older jets’ cabins can also drop below 10%, deliberately to stave off corrosion. Aboard the 787, moisture is less of a worry, so humidity tends to be higher, at between 15% and 25%, contributing to a more comfortable experience for those onboard.

Select Boeing 767 family specifications, from Flightradar24 and Boeing:

Pratt & Whitney JT9D / Pratt & Whitney PW4000 / General Electric CF6

Pratt & Whitney JT9D / Pratt & Whitney PW4000 / General Electric CF6 / Rolls-Royce RB211

Pratt & Whitney JT9D / Pratt & Whitney PW4000 / General Electric CF6 / Rolls-Royce RB211

Pratt & Whitney PW4000 / General Electric CF6

No doubt, Boeing built the 787 to trump its predecessors across the board on efficiency and passenger comfort. The irony is that, in offering a cabin that was wider and more spacious than the 767’s, Boeing effectively gave airlines the choice of squeezing in more seats or giving passengers the extra room. As it turned out, airlines almost universally opted to use the extra width for capacity.

Indeed, Boeing reportedly originally intended the 787 to seat eight passengers per row in economy, in a 2-4-2 configuration. Instead, the 3-3-3 layout has become favored by most airlines. That means it is on the 767, which tends to seat economy travelers in a 2-3-2 pattern, where space is more abundant—despite its narrower fuselage.

United, as an operator of both the 787 and 767, offers a clear example of this. Economy seat width — measured from the inner sides of armrests — across its Dreamliner fleet ranges from approximately 16.6 inches (42.2 centimeters) to 17.6 inches (44.7 centimeters) depending on model and specific interior, per the carrier’s website. Aboard its 767s, this varies between 18.0 inches (45.7 centimeters) and 18.5 inches (47.0 centimeters).

Boeing 767 and Boeing 787 deliveries to date, from Boeing data:

Of course, seat pitch and recline also play a part in determining how much room each passenger gets, and similarly vary from carrier to carrier. That said, the trend of economy seats being wider on 767s than 787s is not limited to United; most carriers put the latter’s wider fuselage to work by installing extra seats.

How do the two airliners differ, and what sets them apart from older aircraft?

Not all do, though. Japan Airlines is a notable exception when it comes to the 787, given its Dreamliner economy cabins feature a seat less per row than at the majority of other carriers. Unsurprisingly, this means the airline’s standard 787 seats are wider than those on its 767s.

Based on figures from the Japanese flag carrier’s website, passengers can expect their economy seat to measure approximately 18.9 inches (48 centimeters) from the inside of one armrest to the other if on one of its 787s. Conversely, this drops to around 17.7 inches (45 centimeters) aboard Japan Airlines’ 767s.

This is because, unlike others, the carrier’s 787s host a 2-4-2 instead of a 3-3-3 configuration in their main cabins. As the airline writes itself: “A more relaxed eight-across seat layout rather than the industry standard nine-across [allows] for an extra five centimeters in seat width.” Compared to Japan Airlines’ 767s, which use the usual 2-3-2 main cabin layout, more of the extra space afforded by the 787’s wider cabin goes to passengers.

All told, Japan Airlines is an outlier when it comes to its 787 seating plan. The bulk of airlines have instead taken to getting the maximum out of the Dreamliner’s width by fitting more passengers per row than on the 767. In other words, the fact that the 787 offers more space between cabin walls does not necessarily mean a more spacious seat onboard in most cases.

There is also the noteworthy fact that 767s tend to feature just one middle seat across each main cabin row. That is impressive not only compared to the 787, but also to even bulkier jets like the Boeing 777, where economy passengers will usually find ten adjacent seats laid out in a 3-4-3 formation.
