My husband and I have always dreamed of visiting London, but we knew we wanted to do it the right way: comfortable flights and a chic hotel stay, with room left in our budget for things like afternoon tea, souvenirs and even a day trip.

All of that can sometimes require some pretty deep pockets, which is why we spent the past year allocating our spending strategically, using my to earn points toward both our flights and our hotel stay.

But like anyone on a budget, we wanted to get the most bang for our “point.” So when American Express last offered a 30% transfer bonus to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers, I knew I had to jump on the opportunity and book our trip asap. The good news? Amex is offering this same transfer bonus to Virgin again, now through Nov. 30, 2026.

Here’s how I made the most of the transfer bonus, including the redemptions I made and how you can do the same with the current offer.

First, let’s break down how the bonus works:

The American Express Membership Rewards® program is offering a 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers until Nov. 30, 2026. That means every 1,000 Membership Rewards points you transfer becomes 1,300 Virgin Points®. Terms apply. Note that Amex points must be transferred in multiples of 1,000, with a minimum of 1,000 points.

Now I’m no math whiz, but I do know that means 100,000 Membership Rewards points would convert to 130,000 Virgin Points, instead of the standard 1:1 ratio. That's one of the best transfer rates Amex offers.

Several Amex cards earn transferable Membership Rewards points, including:

Editor tip: If you’re new to transferring Membership Rewards, like I was, I highly recommend checking out our beginner-friendly guide that breaks down how to transfer Membership Rewards points to partners like Virgin step by step, along with any restrictions you need to be aware of.

The best part about Virgin as a transfer partner is its surprising breadth. You can redeem your points for flights on Virgin Atlantic, as well as stays at Virgin Hotels and cruise sailings with Virgin Voyages.

I had built up a solid balance of Membership Rewards points through a combination of the Gold Card's welcome offer and my everyday spending, but the limited-time window of that bonus meant I couldn't afford to think about it for too long.

I live in Central Florida, and luckily for me, Virgin Atlantic offers nonstop flights from Orlando

International Airport (MCO) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR). However, Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop to LHR from airports across the U.S., including:

Personally, I’ve always been curious about Virgin’s premium economy cabin after hearing so many great things about it from my fellow TPG colleagues. So for our outbound flight, we booked premium economy, which comes with perks like extra legroom and an elevated meal service.

It cost me 35,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. With the 30% bonus, I only needed to transfer 54,000 Amex points for the two of us, which means I saved 16,000 Amex points on the outbound leg alone.

Note that taxes, fees and charges apply in addition to the points price for reward flights in all classes. These vary depending on factors such as your destination and travel dates, and the applicable amount is shown at the time of booking.

From check-in to landing, the premium economy cabin proved to be the perfect balance of value and comfort. Extra touches like a dedicated check-in desk, a glass of bubbly after boarding, upgraded dining and amenity kits made the experience feel so special. The wide leather seats with extra legroom meant we arrived in London well-rested and ready to explore. I could see why so many people rave about it; it was the perfect middle ground between budget-friendly and comfortable.

The real splurge was our return flight, which turned out to hardly be a splurge at all because I found a nonstop Upper Class flight home from LHR to MCO for just 29,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. Thanks to the bonus, I only needed to transfer 46,000 Amex points total for two people. That's 12,000 Membership Reward points saved on an already incredible redemption. Needless to say, I felt like I’d won the lottery.

I’ll be the first to tell you that it doesn’t get any better than Virgin’s Upper Class for R&R on a nine-hour flight across the Atlantic. The direct-aisle-access seats converted into lie-flat beds, and the amenity kits were well curated. Not to mention that the dining and inflight service made me feel like, well, royalty.

By the time we touched down in Orlando, I had slept through most of the flight, which is a rarity for me as a nervous flyer. We arrived home feeling restored rather than depleted.

Combined, our flights cost us 128,000 Virgin Points plus taxes and fees, which took 100,000 Amex points to cover. The transfer bonus saved my husband and me 28,000 Membership Rewards points across both flights, and we used them to redeem on Virgin Red for a rewards stay at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch.

Once I had committed to the Virgin Atlantic booking, staying at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch was a no-brainer with that 30% transfer bonus. And yes, when you transfer Membership Rewards points to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you can use them toward a stay at a Virgin Hotels property.

Editor tip: Once you’ve transferred your Membership Reward points to Virgin,  check out our easy-to-follow guide to booking Virgin Hotels with Virgin Points.

On our dates, the stay came out to about 60,000 Virgin Points per night. For our four-night stay, I was looking at 240,000 points in total, which felt like a lot to give up. With the 30% transfer bonus, though, I only needed to transfer 185,000 Membership Rewards points, which was much easier to wrap my head around.

When I booked the hotel, I had a feeling using my points would be well worth it, and from the moment we arrived at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch, my suspicions were confirmed. The hotel sits in trendy East London, far enough from the crowds and tourist traps, but close to the Old Street Tube station for easy access to activities and dining across the city. It’s also a convenient 10-minute walk from Liverpool Street Station, which has direct access to LHR.

The hotel has quintessential Virgin design, with red accents everywhere, from the lobby carpets to the Smeg fridges in the guest rooms. Beyond the rooms, the property has a rooftop pool for the warmer months and a retro hi-fi listening bar called Hidden Grooves, which serves creative cocktails that are perfect after a long day exploring London.

As for how it compares to cash pricing, a comparable room size runs around $450-$550 per night. Our four-night stay on Virgin Points was equivalent to saving roughly $2,000 in cash, which suddenly made the Amex transfer bonus feel like money in the bank.

With our flights and hotels covered by points, we had cash to spend on our most anticipated experiences in London. Here are a few of my favorite trip highlights:

My Membership Rewards transfer to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club covered nearly every big-ticket item on our London trip: flights in both directions, including a lie-flat Upper Class seat home, and four nights at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch. With the 30% transfer bonus stretching every point further, we were able to spend our cash on experiences, dining and souvenirs.

If you've been sitting on a stash of Membership Rewards points, this is one of the best ways to use them right now, and you don’t need to go to London. Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop from the U.S. to Manchester and Edinburgh and connecting through Heathrow opens up destinations like Barbados, Cape Town, Dubai, Mumbai and the Maldives.

Your points aren't limited to flights, either. You can put them toward a stay at Virgin Hotels or even a Virgin Voyages cruise. Just keep in mind that the 30% transfer bonus, available to eligible U.S. cardmembers, ends Nov. 30, 2026, so whether you're dreaming of a lie-flat seat across the Atlantic or days in the sun at sea, now is the time to book your next trip.

The National Review newsletter captured a time in which revolutionary violence tried to join the mainstream.

Young men raise their fists and chant slogans during the “Days of Rage” demonstrations organized by the Weatherman to protest the Chicago Seven trial and “to bring the war home” in Chicago, Ill., in 1969.

Socialism looks in 2026 a lot like bell bottoms: tried on, worn out, and out of fashion.

Decades ago, Germany, Russia, Cambodia, Ethiopia, and points beyond tried socialism to disastrous results. Many American leftists, as judged by the election returns, believe in an American exceptionalism of sorts, too. They think that socialism in the United States will be different. We won’t need a world war, societal collapse, or the obligatory charitable single and accompanying global benefit show to save us from its consequences. Socialism, for its true believers, amounts to salvation and not that from which people living under it require deliverance.

#6123. Beond Airlines Suspends Flights For The Rest Of The Year: Better Luck In 2027?

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of late October. Then in October, it announced it would return in December. There’s now another update, as the airline has just announced that it will resume flights in January. That doesn’t sound so good, does it?

Beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The company is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline currently has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Then in October, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Then just yesterday, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through December 31, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of January 1, 2027.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of January, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. If you can’t make all-business class flights to the Maldives work for the festive season, then prospects seem pretty grim.

Beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when plans change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business plan was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

As I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in January. I wouldn’t count on it. One bizarre angle to this is that Beond has claimed it will launch flights to London Heathrow (LHR). Best I can tell, there’s no public record of the airline getting slots for that. And if the airline did have slots, it would be under a “use it or lose it” clause, so not operating the route would make the airline lose them.

In the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. Then the airline announced it would resume flights in December 2026. Now the airline claims it will relaunch flights in January 2027. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

We’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?

#6122. Former Hyatt Renovation Halted After Inspectors Find Families Living Inside—And Rooms Chained From The Outside

Inspectors entered the closed former Hyatt Regency Dearborn and found families living upstairs. Hotel room doors on the property were chained and padlocked from the outside. Two days later, police searched. The families were gone. Officers closed the case after about a two hour search. On September 22, inspectors found, On the 12th floor: Dozens of people, including young children, with groceries, suitcases, puppies and dog feces. On the 10th floor: Doors chained and padlocked from outside, apparently impossible to unlock from within. In a hallway: Packaging for a large machete (though no machete was seen). A project manager initially suggested a worker’s family was visiting for lunch. A guard said up to 100 people had lived there over the previous year, and his bosses told him to ignore residents. The hotel’s owner denied knowing families were living there. Police said the locked rooms secured workers’ equipment and their search found no criminal activity, such as human trafficking. This is the Edward Hotel and Convention Center which once had a revolving restaurant and a monorail connection to Fairlane Town Center. It left Hyatt in 2012, and the city shut it down in 2018. The property was acquired in 2016 for $20 million. That owner faced criminal charges in Canada that were ultimately withdrawn. It was sold in 2021 in a forfeiture sale for $18.25 million. The buyer defaulted on the mortgage and in 2024 it was auctioned by the sheriff for $9.85 million, but apparently an auction of the distressed note and sheriff’s deed ended at $5.925 million. According to Dearborn City Council materials from October 2024, Hyatt had expressed interest in returning if sufficient capital investment could be secured. This exterior photo is from September 2024, by Warren LeMay via Wikipedia. But Wait, It Gets Worse According to a local activist a supposed immigration agent had thrown someone to the floor and killed a dog by throwing it through glass. She later reached an injured woman inside, who told her: “I don’t know how to get out.” The activist also said workers reported wages withheld because employers supposedly used the money to bribe immigration agents and being told: “Look, we’re keeping ICE away from you. Now you have to work for free.” Immigration and Customs Enforcement denies conducting enforcement at the hotel. A Detroit councilwoman’s office says Mayor Abdullah Hammoud was alerted September 18, four days before the inspection. Reportedly police failed to review the hotel’s surveillance video before closing the investigation. The Hotel Was Supposed To Make A Comeback Dearborn has sunk subsidies into the hotel’s redevelopment plans. In December 2025, the city approved a 12-year property tax exemption and a 30-year brownfield plan for a redevelopment involving a $45 million rehabilitation, plus acquisition costs. The project would combine hotel rooms, apartments and convention space. In January, the mayor said the hotel would return as a Hilton, with a hoped-for opening by the end of 2026. Here’s a walk-through of the property from before the current state of affairs: I don’t think the former Hyatt Regency Dearborn is re-opening as a Hilton in 2026. It strikes me that the city isn’t adequately investigating issues at a redevelopment site that it’s subsidizing. A project manager initially suggested a worker’s family was visiting for lunch. A guard said up to 100 people had lived there over the previous year, and his bosses told him to ignore residents. The hotel’s owner denied knowing families were living there.

Police said the locked rooms secured workers’ equipment and their search found no criminal activity, such as human trafficking.

This is the Edward Hotel and Convention Center which once had a revolving restaurant and a monorail connection to Fairlane Town Center. It left Hyatt in 2012, and the city shut it down in 2018.

The property was acquired in 2016 for $20 million. That owner faced criminal charges in Canada that were ultimately withdrawn. It was sold in 2021 in a forfeiture sale for $18.25 million. The buyer defaulted on the mortgage and in 2024 it was auctioned by the sheriff for $9.85 million, but apparently an auction of the distressed note and sheriff’s deed ended at $5.925 million. According to Dearborn City Council materials from October 2024, Hyatt had expressed interest in returning if sufficient capital investment could be secured. This exterior photo is from September 2024, by Warren LeMay via Wikipedia. #6121. Delta 360: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

All of the “big three” carriers in the United States have invitation-only elite status. I’ve written about how American has Concierge Key and United has Global Services, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at Delta 360, which is Delta’s invitation-only elite status. I’d argue it’s the most mysterious, least talked about, and perhaps the rarest, of the three.

What is Delta 360 status, how do you earn it, what are the benefits, and how many members are there? I’ll share everything I know…

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite status. It’s my understanding that this is the most exclusive of the invitation-only elite tiers, in the sense that there are the fewest members. Despite that, the benefits are actually pretty weak, at least on paper. For that matter, Delta 360 isn’t even a formal elite tier, which is to say that you separately still have to qualify for status in the Delta SkyMiles Medallion program.

For what it’s worth, here’s how Delta describes Delta 360 status on its website:

Delta 360° is an annual, invitation-only membership for our most loyal SkyMiles Members. A Delta 360° Membership offers Delta’s most premium suite of benefits and services exclusive to our top SkyMiles Members. Entry into Delta 360° will be extended to a very small percentage of Diamond Medallion Members. Considerations include, but are not limited to: overall Delta flight activity, premium product purchases (Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta First) and spending on Delta SkyMiles American Express Cards.

As is the case with the invitation-only status of American and United, the requirements to earn Delta 360 status aren’t published. However, based on the data points I’ve seen, the criteria are even more confusing. With American and United, as a general rule, you need to spend well over $50,000 per year to have a shot at the status. In the case of Delta, you probably need to spend even more.

As Delta officially states, getting an invitation to Delta 360 is for the “most loyal SkyMiles members.” Generally speaking:

Some suggest that you’d have to spend $100,000 per year on Delta flights to be invited as a Delta 360 member at major hubs, while the number could be much lower if you’re not based at a hub.

Note that qualification for Delta 360 is annual (so it expires at the end of the elite year), and criteria could change year-to-year. So it’s possible you have the same activity in two years, and earn Delta 360 one year, but not the other. There’s also no way to ask for or request the status (at least not in a way that will achieve the intended result). Instead, you’ll be contacted if you’re eligible, and you’ll see your account updated to reflect that.

There’s one other way to earn Delta 360 status. As part of the SkyMiles lifetime elite status program, you can receive Delta 360 status for life if you rack up five million lifetime miles. This metric is based on the number of eligible miles flown on Delta.

Just for some context on all of this, Delta’s top published tier is Diamond Medallion, and that requires earning 28,000 Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs) in a program year. That would require $28,000 in spending on Delta tickets, or $280,000 to $560,000 in spending on select co-branded Delta credit cards.

Interestingly, Delta 360 isn’t a separate tier in the SkyMiles program. That’s to say that Delta 360 members still have to earn status in the SkyMiles Medallion program. Most Delta 360 members are also Diamond Medallion members, but in theory it’s possible to earn Delta 360 without being a Diamond Medallion member.

This is different than American AAdvantage and United MileagePlus, where Concierge Key and Global Services are separate tiers, above the published top tier levels.

What are the benefits of Delta 360 status?

Those are all the Delta 360 benefits that I’m aware of. There’s no upgrade priority for Delta 360 members beyond their standard Diamond Medallion status, so Delta 360 doesn’t factor into upgrade priority. Furthermore, any confirmed upgrades would be earned through the standard Choice Benefits program, as this is how you can earn Global Upgrade Certificates (GUCs) and Regional Upgrade Certificates (RUCs).

So the benefits of Delta 360 are weak, though I’d imagine that the “soft” treatment is very good — Delta has great service to begin with, and I imagine it’s even better for Delta’s best customers.

I also think it’s noteworthy how Delta is much quieter about this status than American and United. There’s just not as much public acknowledgement of invitation only status at Delta as at American and United (and that might be by design).

This is a real mystery, and all I can do is speculate. For context, I’ve speculated that there are 10,000-20,000 American Concierge Key members, and I’ve speculated that there are 15,000-25,000 United Global Services members.

This is purely a guess on my part, but I think the number of Delta 360 members is probably in the 5,000-10,000 range. That’s simply because the status seems to be more difficult to earn. Like I said, this is purely a guess on my part, and I could be wrong. If anyone has any data or info, I’d love to hear it.

It’s hard to say whether something like Delta 360 is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Delta 360 varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Delta One Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal, above and beyond what you’d otherwise get.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including American Concierge Key and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, I’d say Delta 360 probably offers the fewest official perks of the three tiers. The one exception is that Delta One Lounge access is an absolutely awesome benefit, given the quality of lounges (though the lack of free guests limits the usefulness for those not usually traveling alone).

Here are a couple of thoughts on the comparable status tiers at American and United:

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite tier. It’s the US airline status that’s probably hardest to earn. Historically the benefits have been weaker than comparable status with American and United, though with access to Delta One Lounges, that’s perhaps no longer the case. Delta 360 offers dedicated customer support, a Sky Club membership, Delta One Lounge access, good odds of tarmac transfers, and more.

To earn Delta 360, be prepared to spend a lot on Delta flights, especially if you’re based out of a Delta hub.

Are any OMAAT readers Delta 360 members? If so, what has your experience been like?

Membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

#6120. The Republican Party Must Be Bigger Than Any One Person

The GOP’s future depends on putting principles first.

President Ronald Reagan gives his acceptance speech at the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas

In 1967, Ronald Reagan offered a reminder about the Republican Party that is as relevant today as it was nearly 60 years ago: “Unity does not require unanimity of thought.” Reagan understood something fundamental about political leadership: A party is not a personality cult. It is a coalition of Americans united by shared principles, even when they disagree about policy specifics.

In the aftermath of the midterm elections, Republicans have serious questions to confront. The results demand reflection and an examination of what we believe and what kind of political institution we intend to be. I believe in the Constitution, limited government, individual liberty, fiscal responsibility, and personal accountability. Those convictions have not changed because of political pressure, nor are they dependent on who occupies the White House.

President Ronald Reagan gives his acceptance speech at the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas

Brad Raffensperger is the secretary of state for Georgia.

#6118. FAA Ground Stop: Every U.S. Airport Departure Halted As Air Traffic Control Communications Fail

The FAA has ordered departures stopped at every U.S. airport after a communications failure hit air traffic control centers across the country. Planes are being held on the ground as Friday afternoon travelers head into the weekend, with no announced time for flights to resume. Aircraft already in the air are being allowed to continue and land. There isn’t a general order to put every plane down at the nearest airport, like 9/11. The FAA says inbound international flights will be handled individually. The agency’s national ground stop advisory, issued at 3:54 p.m. Eastern on November 13: DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS. The FAA’s status board lists the reason as “EQUIPMENT / OUTAGE.” This is in place “until further notice.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirms a communications issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers, with FAA technicians investigating. These are the facilities that handle aircraft flying between airport areas. Secretary Sean Duffy’s statement — November 13, 2026 Aviation watchdog JonNYC reported widespread frequency failures before the nationwide order. His initial reports named Boston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center and New York Approach, with Boston Approach also experiencing problems. Some New York Center sectors reportedly couldn’t accept traffic. Then things spread. Chicago O’Hare and Midway were placed under ground stops before the nationwide halt. JonNYC’s reports of air traffic control frequency failures — November 13, 2026 A cockpit message shared by JonNYC tells crews: ATTENTION ALL CREWS- PER FAA GUIDANCE, ALL DEPARTURES ARE STOPPED NATIONWIDE. PLEASE STANDBY FOR FURTHER INFORMATION. UPDATE IN 15 https://t.co/XQvj5neLF2 — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 13, 2026 A Software Upgrade Issue Has Been Reported The New York Post reports that an unnamed source points to a possible software upgrade behind the disruption. The FAA hasn’t identified the failed system or what triggered the outage. However, controller and pilot message boards have several more specific accounts. In Reddit’s air traffic control forum, one commenter writes, “Allegedly all [backup emergency communications] sites on the east coast went out at the same time. They’re trying to figure out why.” Another commenter describes those backups as a third radio system, with separate radios, antennas, power and communications links. If the reported simultaneous failures are accurate, the behavior of those backups becomes a particularly important part of the investigation. In a second controller forum, a poster reports, “A lot of the frequencies and landlines in the Houston area started going hot on their own randomly over the past hour.” That adds a report of unexpected activity on both radio and telephone connections. In the flying forum, a commenter says the word they’re hearing is a communications problem between en route facilities. Others report hearing controllers announce the nationwide stop in Seattle and Redmond. JonNYC reports facilities preparing for “ATC Zero,” the status used when a facility can’t provide air traffic services. The FAA Has A Long History Of Technology Failures The closest recent comparison is the January 11, 2023 nationwide ground stop, when the system that provides safety notices to pilots failed. The FAA later traced that outage to contractors accidentally deleting files while trying to correct synchronization between the primary database and a backup. That was only the second nationwide ground stop, after 9/11. In March I covered an overheated circuit board that disrupted five Washington area airports. Transportation researcher Bob Poole reported that the board was part of a 25 year old voice switch, describing an FAA maintenance policy that allowed equipment to run until it failed, with fewer technicians and inadequate training to keep old systems going. The FAA’s own equipment photos illustrate what they’ve been working with: When I reviewed the administration’s air traffic control overhaul, the plan called for replacing 25,000 analog radios and 800 voice switches, along with moving thousands of sites off legacy telecommunications connections. My criticism was that the same organization that spent decades failing to deliver upgrades would be asked to deliver another one. The FAA regulates itself, both running the system and regulating its safety, while long term capital projects depend on annual congressional appropriations. Buying equipment doesn’t fix bad incentives or project management. Earlier today, the administration asked Congress for another $30.1 billion in aviation funding, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. The new request also includes money for control towers and airport projects. They want taxpayers bailing out the system, rather than airlines and passengers. Even a quick repair won’t immediately put the airlines back on schedule. Planes held now will be late for their next flights, connecting passengers will miss departures, and crews can run out of permitted duty time. Then with planes out of position, disruptions continue. They want taxpayers bailing out the system, rather than airlines and passengers. Even a quick repair won’t immediately put the airlines back on schedule. Planes held now will be late for their next flights, connecting passengers will miss departures, and crews can run out of permitted duty time. Then with planes out of position, disruptions continue. Topics on this pageAir traffic controlFederal Aviation AdministrationGround stopHoustonNew York PostO'Hare International AirportRedditRobert PooleSean DuffySeattleUnited States Congress+8 more More From View from the Wing

The closest recent comparison is the January 11, 2023 nationwide ground stop, when the system that provides safety notices to pilots failed. The FAA later traced that outage to contractors accidentally deleting files while trying to correct synchronization between the primary database and a backup. That was only the second nationwide ground stop, after 9/11.

In March I covered an overheated circuit board that disrupted five Washington area airports. Transportation researcher Bob Poole reported that the board was part of a 25 year old voice switch, describing an FAA maintenance policy that allowed equipment to run until it failed, with fewer technicians and inadequate training to keep old systems going.

The FAA’s own equipment photos illustrate what they’ve been working with:

When I reviewed the administration’s air traffic control overhaul, the plan called for replacing 25,000 analog radios and 800 voice switches, along with moving thousands of sites off legacy telecommunications connections.

My criticism was that the same organization that spent decades failing to deliver upgrades would be asked to deliver another one. The FAA regulates itself, both running the system and regulating its safety, while long term capital projects depend on annual congressional appropriations. Buying equipment doesn’t fix bad incentives or project management.

Earlier today, the administration asked Congress for another $30.1 billion in aviation funding, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. The new request also includes money for control towers and airport projects. They want taxpayers bailing out the system, rather than airlines and passengers.

Even a quick repair won’t immediately put the airlines back on schedule. Planes held now will be late for their next flights, connecting passengers will miss departures, and crews can run out of permitted duty time. Then with planes out of position, disruptions continue.

#6113. Iran Is Still a Menace

A member of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps at a military training center for citizens in Tehran, Iran, November 2, 2026.

Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters

The American public may not be interested in the Iran war, but it is still interested in us.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his home to a military base after credible Iranian threats against his life. Bessent helps oversee the crippling financial sanctions imposed on Iran, making him a particular target for the regime.

In the past several years, former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Adviser John Bolton, and President Trump himself have also been the targets of Iranian assassination plots.

With the Iran war playing a prominent role in the GOP’s stunning defeat in last week’s elections, there is renewed pressure — both from incoming Democrats and critics on the right — to put an end to the conflict.

On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that JD Vance had become lead negotiator with Iran, to the point of even contemplating direct talks with a top Iranian security official. The same article related that Trump had started to second-guess the wisdom of the June memorandum of understanding that Vance negotiated and that Trump gladly signed, wondering whether it allowed time for Iran to regroup and earn more oil revenue.

On Thursday morning, Trump, who has been vacillating between threatening to bomb Iran and touting imminent peace almost by the day, poured cold water on the idea of any renewed negotiations. The president took to Truth Social to say that he was asking Vance to focus on corruption in Democrat-run cities. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Bombast aside, a status quo in which the U.S. maintains a naval blockade against Iran and escorts ships through the Strait of Hormuz may be the least bad of the remaining options. While maintaining that pressure, the U.S. should also look for ways to actively support the Iranian opposition, something President Trump implicitly promised in January with his “help is on its way” comments. But we obviously cannot bank on the Iranian regime falling or moderating any time soon. It is hard to see what can be accomplished strategically through another weeks-long air campaign, but the immediate diplomatic prospects are dim, as well.

Presumably, any deal that Iran would agree to in the aftermath of what it considers its victory in the midterms would be a bad one for the U.S., likely a repeat of Barack Obama’s disastrous Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, if not worse. Under that agreement, Iran enjoyed hundreds of billions of dollars in sanctions relief, preserved its ability to enrich uranium, and maintained its ballistic missile program. The scandal of the Iran deal was that even if it worked exactly as intended, it would have still allowed Iran to continue to develop a more powerful conventional military, to sponsor terrorism, and to exert a malign influence within the region and around the world. All the while, restrictions on its nuclear program were set to expire over time, putting the regime on a long-term glide path to weaponization. If any eventual agreements are to be reached with Iran, they must meet two tests: First, do no harm, and second, trade nothing for any promises of future conduct by the Iranians.

Iran’s plots against one of the most important U.S. cabinet officials, as well as Americans throughout the Middle East, underline the malignity of an Iranian regime that has been in a conflict with the United States for a half century. In short, it is still very interested in the war, and in doing us harm.

American Airlines is planning to add more flights from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), as part of a “gradual build” at its West Coast hub.

The Fort Worth-based carrier said it's about to add more LAX service to its schedule, with a focus on places executives describe as “important markets.”

It’s not clear whether that means entirely new routes or more frequent service on existing ones.

But either way, it comes after a long stretch where American seemed to focus far more of its attention on other parts of the country.

After the pandemic, the airline doubled down on its Sun Belt hubs, fortifying its strongholds in Dallas, Charlotte and Miami.

More recently, American reignited a longstanding Chicago turf war with United Airlines when it rapidly reinstated flying at O’Hare International Airport (ORD).

It looks like LAX will be its next project.

“We’re going to grow," American chief commercial officer Nat Pieper said, speaking this week at an industry conference. "We’re going to tailor a schedule to the local market."

American has a smaller presence today in Southern California than it did several years ago.

This year, the carrier will operate about 32% fewer flights than it did in 2019, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

That’s a significant drop-off at LAX, which is one of the nation’s most competitive airports — and the only where each of the “big three” legacy carriers operates a hub.

By contrast, top L.A. rival Delta Air Lines has solidified its place as the airport’s top carrier, and plans operate its largest-ever schedule there next year.

United Airlines has also signaled it has future growth aspirations at LAX.

Speaking earlier this year, United’s top network planner, Patrick Quayle, lamented the fact that the airport is United’s only hub where there’s another airline with a larger presence.

“I don’t like being No. 2,” Quayle said during a company event at LAX in March. “And so I will, today, put Delta on notice here in L.A. — we will be No. 1, as well.”'

Pieper said the carrier needs to start by catering more to local Los Angeles customers — not just using the airport as a hub to route connecting traffic.

Doing that, he acknowledged, will likely require AA to offer a longer list of unique destinations.

Today, for instance, the carrier only serves four long-haul cities from LAX: London, Tokyo, Sydney and Auckland.

“People don’t only want to fly domestically. They want to go to Latin America. They want to go to Europe. They want to go to Asia,” Pieper said on stage this week at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York. “We need to be able to serve that with our own airplanes.”

United is clearly following that formula. The carrier already serves more than a half-dozen transpacific destinations from Southern California — and will expand next year with a new route to Osaka.

Delta, for its part, is also pointing to LAX as a linchpin of its Pacific growth aspirations, having launched nonstops to Hong Kong and Melbourne within the past year. New flights to Manila will begin in 2027.

Delta’s Los Angeles growth is also thanks, in part, to massive infrastructure investments the carrier has made at the hub which, among other things, is the only airport that's home to two Delta One Lounges.

American’s LAX digs, meanwhile, are still a construction zone.

The carrier had to consolidate its presence at the airport last year to make way for a rebuild of the airport's Terminal 5.

American will grow at a "gradual" pace, Pieper said, until its LAX facilities are "ready to roll." That's expected to happen in late 2028, at which point the carrier will have access to 30 gates.

“Our facility will be as good as anybody’s,” he said.

That, along with more flights — plus connectivity to American's Pacific partners like Qantas and Japan Airlines— have the airline more bullish about its hub that's grabbed far fewer headlines in recent years.

“You combine all those things together,” Pieper added, “I think we’re going to have a compelling offering there.”

A Japanese woman screams “Help me!” and “SOS!” as border officers handcuff her at Honolulu airport. Her Hawaii trip ends with a rush to get her onto a flight back to Nagoya leaving in 30 minutes because missing it would mean spending the night in federal detention. Newly circulating footage of the incident comes from Frontline Crime uploaded in July, and is from an episode of Airport Security: USA that appears to have come out two years ago. A report on the clip describes the woman as a Japanese ‘hostess’. View the airport footage shared by Grit Hiro The woman refused to cooperate with a request to move to secondary inspection. Officers restrain her as she cries out and insists she’s visiting on vacation. An officer says they were asking basic questions when she accused them of suspecting her of prostitution. He treats that reaction as evidence that she has something to hide. Questioning eventually turns to who paid for her airfare and hotel. She says a man covered the trip, but she doesn’t know where he is and hasn’t contacted him. The narrator first says officers suspect he has ties to a Japanese criminal organization, then reports an organized crime connection. The officer declares she hasn’t overcome the presumption that she intends to immigrate, and tells her she’ll be sent back to Japan because that makes her ineligible to enter as a temporary visitor. If she intended to work in a Hawaii club, even just serving drinks and talking with customers would be a problem because she was entering as a tourist and not someone work authorized. On Japanese Twitter, Hiroyuki Nishimura mocked the idea that refusing questions and making a scene would get her admitted. I’ve covered Molly Hill, who said she was strip searched and jailed after flying to Hawaii to visit her boyfriend. She had a ticket home after 88 days. Officials suspected she intended to stay, and she was brought back through the airport in handcuffs on her birthday. And in 2022, an Australian traveler was detained in Honolulu over an onward-ticket problem. Newly circulating footage of the incident comes from Frontline Crime uploaded in July, and is from an episode of Airport Security: USA that appears to have come out two years ago.

A report on the clip describes the woman as a Japanese ‘hostess’.

View the airport footage shared by Grit Hiro

The woman refused to cooperate with a request to move to secondary inspection. Officers restrain her as she cries out and insists she’s visiting on vacation. An officer says they were asking basic questions when she accused them of suspecting her of prostitution. He treats that reaction as evidence that she has something to hide.

Questioning eventually turns to who paid for her airfare and hotel. She says a man covered the trip, but she doesn’t know where he is and hasn’t contacted him. The narrator first says officers suspect he has ties to a Japanese criminal organization, then reports an organized crime connection. The officer declares she hasn’t overcome the presumption that she intends to immigrate, and tells her she’ll be sent back to Japan because that makes her ineligible to enter as a temporary visitor.

If she intended to work in a Hawaii club, even just serving drinks and talking with customers would be a problem because she was entering as a tourist and not someone work authorized. On Japanese Twitter, Hiroyuki Nishimura mocked the idea that refusing questions and making a scene would get her admitted.

I’ve covered Molly Hill, who said she was strip searched and jailed after flying to Hawaii to visit her boyfriend. She had a ticket home after 88 days. Officials suspected she intended to stay, and she was brought back through the airport in handcuffs on her birthday.

And in 2022, an Australian traveler was detained in Honolulu over an onward-ticket problem. Jack Dunn said he was strip searched, placed in a cell, and left to sleep on a concrete floor with a paper bag for a pillow.

#6108. The Week: Jensen Huang, Honeytrapped

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang speaks with the media ahead of a meeting with the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., December 3, 2025.

• China has gained an edge in one of the world’s most dangerous technologies: the honeypot.

• Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the tech giant Nvidia, as news of extramarital affairs with multiple subordinates and a spy scandal engulfed the company. The “other woman” in the honeytrap has been identified in numerous reports as a Chinese national and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company in the business of renting out computing power that relies on Nvidia’s advanced chips (which it has bought in huge quantities). U.S. intelligence has accused Megaspeed of smuggling contraband chips to China and identified the Nvidia CEO’s paramour as a Chinese spy, information that was passed on to senior officials in Washington. The FBI and Congress are taking a closer look. Nvidia’s advanced chips are absolutely critical for cutting-edge AI models, so handling this scandal will be complicated. We are ahead of China in the AI “arms race” to a degree that an effort dominated by the government would not match, but it’s a lead that Washington, if it mishandles its response to this mess, could all too easily undermine. We do, however, need once again to examine what chips U.S. companies may sell to China. The efforts that the Chinese appear to be making to get hold of a U.S. product make the case for not selling it to them. Huang has argued that if the U.S. withholds more advanced chips, the Chinese will develop their own. They will try to do so anyway. Beijing’s instincts are autarkic. There is no sense in the U.S. making that task any easier.

• China has gained an edge in one of the world’s most dangerous technologies: the honeypot.

• Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the tech giant Nvidia, as news of extramarital affairs with multiple subordinates and a spy scandal engulfed the company. The “other woman” in the honeytrap has been identified in numerous reports as a Chinese national and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company in the business of renting out computing power that relies on Nvidia’s advanced chips (which it has bought in huge quantities). U.S. intelligence has accused Megaspeed of smuggling contraband chips to China and identified the Nvidia CEO’s paramour as a Chinese spy, information that was passed on to senior officials in Washington. The FBI and Congress are taking a closer look. Nvidia’s advanced chips are absolutely critical for cutting-edge AI models, so handling this scandal will be complicated. We are ahead of China in the AI “arms race” to a degree that an effort dominated by the government would not match, but it’s a lead that Washington, if it mishandles its response to this mess, could all too easily undermine. We do, however, need once again to examine what chips U.S. companies may sell to China. The efforts that the Chinese appear to be making to get hold of a U.S. product make the case for not selling it to them. Huang has argued that if the U.S. withholds more advanced chips, the Chinese will develop their own. They will try to do so anyway. Beijing’s instincts are autarkic. There is no sense in the U.S. making that task any easier.

#6107. United CEO Scott Kirby Says “100%” Chance Merger With American Airlines Would Get Approved

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby says he’s “100%” convinced a merger with American Airlines could get approved. He says he’s even more confident than he was this spring, when news of the talks came out, and he sees getting American to agree as the biggest obstacle. But ‘get approved’ doesn’t mean what he seems to suggest. A friendly Justice Department signing off would still leave any such combination with state attorneys general, foreign governments and two competing sets of international airline partnerships to deal with. Speaking at Yahoo Finance Invest, Kirby said: “It wouldn’t be easy.” “We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.” His argument is that bringing United’s service, technology and operational performance to more passengers would make them better off. He thinks critics misunderstand the deal because they treat airline seats as interchangeable. Contra Kirby, better service is actually a core part of DOJ merger guidelines recognizing quality, innovation and choice. Plus, United service isn’t that good! And while their operations are better than they used to be, they aren’t industry-leading. They’re consistently modestly better than American’s but the difference is hardly vast. Kirby Hasn’t Given Up On The Airline That Fired Him When I covered Kirby’s merger pitch in April, the appeal to United was obvious: American would give them a much bigger New York presence, more strength in Los Angeles, a southeastern hub and a powerful Latin America network. Kirby later said he’d build a Miami hub if he could get 40 or 50 gates. He also wants more at New York JFK than United’s planned return will provide. American rejected merger discussions, arguing that combining the airlines would hurt consumers and competition. Any antitrust case – even at the state level – would just quote American’s own release. As I covered October 31, Kirby described conversations he thought were continuing until American blindsided him with that press release. In any case, American can make investments without being bought. They’ve already made real progress over the past 21 months towards improving their product almost across-the-board. The Justice Department Doesn’t Get The Only Vote I laid out the problems beyond Washington back in April. Getting the administration to support a deal isn’t even close to enough. States can bring their own case. A federal settlement doesn’t bind state attorneys general who aren’t parties to it. Private plaintiffs can sue, too. The Clayton Act allows injunctions against threatened antitrust harm. Closing doesn’t automatically end the risk. The merger notification statute preserves later challenges. Letting the federal waiting period expire isn’t permanent antitrust immunity. He’d Have To Untangle Two Competing Global Networks American and US Airways needed European Commission clearance for their merger. The London–Philadelphia remedy included slots for a competing daily flight. Two U.S. companies combining doesn’t make the transaction solely an American matter. United and American also have joint ventures that let them coordinate prices, schedules and revenue with different foreign airlines. Among those arrangements: Market United’s Partners American’s Partners Atlantic   Lufthansa Group and Air Canada   British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus and Finnair Japan   All Nippon Airways   Japan Airlines South Pacific   Air New Zealand   Qantas A combined airline couldn’t assume it could keep these competing arrangements unchanged. Moving American’s flying into United’s partnerships would change the competition analysis. Ending American’s existing deals would also change the connecting traffic and economics Kirby is buying. The Transportation Department’s alliance approvals are another process, separate from Justice Department merger review. And foreign oversight is already an issue: Britain. American’s existing Atlantic partnership already faces slot remedies for London–Boston, London–Chicago and London–Miami, plus protections for London–Dallas passengers. In February, the British competition authority announced approved slot agreements for Delta on Boston and Virgin Atlantic on Miami. Buying American could create new hurdles for either transatlantic joint venture the combined carrier participated in. The European Union would have its own merger review, too. Japan. United and American have separate immunized partnerships with Japan’s two major network airlines. The merger would also raise questions about their scarce Tokyo Haneda access. Japan might not approve a combined American and United in either partnership. Keeping both carriers’ Haneda slots aren’t necessarily in the DOT’s view of the public interest. Australia and New Zealand. Australia renewed the American–Qantas alliance authorization on October 14. New Zealand renewed it in March, and separately authorizes United’s cooperation with Air New Zealand. Combining the American partners in those competing relationships would give both governments new questions to consider regardless of which airline they decided they wanted to keep a partnership with. Canada. United and Air Canada announced an expanded transborder agreement last month and submitted it to Transport Canada for approval. Combining that operation with American’s Canada seems almost impossible on its own. What Would United Have To Give Up? Chicago is the biggest domestic problem. United and American operate competing hubs at O’Hare. New York, Los Angeles and Washington raise challenges as well. United has Newark while American considers the combined LaGuardia and JFK a hub; both airlines have hubs at LAX, and United has a hub at Washington Dulles while American is the dominant carrier at Washington National. And surely American’s debt is a poison pill? It ended September with $29.6 billion in debt and finance leases (without operating leases and pension obligations). The “100% approved” isn’t at all credible, unless he means only at the federal level and because he’s had assurances from the President (who could change his mind!). We didn’t have to wait long to find out how American Airlines is shaking up its route map in Los Angeles.

Just minutes after TPG reported the carrier was planning a route announcement at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), American revealed its plans. And there’s both good and bad news for AA flyers in Southern California.

Most notably, the carrier plans to bolster its service on four routes to major U.S. cities.

It’s also bringing back a route to Colorado that it hasn’t offered in a half-decade.

Plus, American will end service to two cities from LAX.

All told, Friday's changes cover nine routes from its West Coast hub. Here's what to know.

American confirmed it’s bringing back service to Grand Junction, Colorado, for the first time in five years.

It will operate seasonal regional service from LAX between May 27 and Aug. 9 with a Bombardier CRJ700.

American last operated LAX service to Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) in 2021, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

In 2027, this route will effectively replace American’s flight to Colorado’s Aspen/Pitkin County Airport (ASE), which will be closed next summer for construction.

American will fly its LAX-GJT route with one of its smaller CRJ-700 aircraft.

Elsewhere, American will turn to two routes it’s previously offered seasonally — and sporadically —from LAX into more regular service:

Both routes will operate with an Embraer 175 regional jet.

Starting next spring, American will also add extra daily flights from LAX to several major U.S. cities.

Denver, Las Vegas and Seattle will all get additional frequencies. Plus, American will double its daily service on one transcontinental route — from LA to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Starting in May, American will offer twice-daily Dulles service. That’ll make the IAD-LAX routes a stronger complement to AA’s cross-country Los Angeles service from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

American will cut ties with its LAX route to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) effective Feb. 11.

That same day, it will also end service to Des Moines, Iowa.

This network revamp in LA comes a day after American executives said the carrier was rethinking the routes it offers at its Southern California hub.

American’s LAX service today sharply lags the flight offerings it had at the airport in 2019.

Speaking Thursday, American’s chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, said the airline would aim to offer more flights from LAX to major U.S. cities in a push to win more L.A.-based flyers.

"We’re going to grow and we’re going to invest in the local market,” he said, speaking Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York.

That expansion, Pieper noted, will be gradual — and ramp up — as infrastructure work at LAX progresses over the next two years.

#6102. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

Some of the most aspirational business-class award redemptions are increasingly hard to find, even for the most experienced points and miles enthusiasts.

Cathay Pacific is a prime example. It's harder and harder to find award availability in the Hong Kong-based airline's premium cabins, especially with partners.

But one trick still works: Look for award availability when airlines launch new routes or bring back old ones.

I was able to fly from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points. That is a screaming deal. But there was only saver-level availability for a limited time when the schedule was first loaded.

It turned out to be a fantastic redemption, with excellent service, delicious food and a comfortable lie-flat seat for the long journey across the Pacific.

I'll have more details later in this story on how to find some of these incredible deals in business class, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

Here's what my experience was like aboard Cathay Pacific's Airbus A350-900 and how you can use a similar strategy to find these elusive business-class awards.

Cathay Pacific relaunched its service to Hong Kong from Seattle in March 2026, after suspending the route during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The route originally launched in March 2019 and was canceled in November of the following year. The airline's CEO told TPG that the carrier had always wanted to restore the route, which was Seattle's first nonstop service to Hong Kong since the pandemic.

The plane was a nine-year-old A350-900 with the ship number B-LRL, with 38 business-class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 214 economy seats.

It was a very comfortable way to cross the Pacific and opens up fun new ways to get to Asia from the U.S. West Coast. It also adds another way to use points and miles to fly to Hong Kong, though as you'll read below, it's no easy task to find the lowest-level award availability.

Business-class guests on Cathay Pacific are invited to use The Club at Seattle in the South Satellite area, which is connected to the main terminal by an underground train.

The Club SEA is an independent lounge that participates in Priority Pass. It offers a buffet of hot and cold food items and free drinks. It's basic, and it doesn't hold a candle to Cathay Pacific's own lounges in places like San Francisco and Hong Kong (no noodle bar here). However, it will do the trick for a quick drink and bite.

It was crowded during my quick visit, and I didn't spend much time at this lounge, since I'd had access to the beautiful Alaska Airlines lounge in the N Concourse. I grabbed a bite there before heading to the S Concourse, which is about to get a major, modern $2.5 billion renovation. It should be a much nicer place to hang out once the renovations are done.

Cathay Pacific has 38 business-class seats, split between two cabins. I was in the forward cabin with 30 seats arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration. There is a smaller cabin with just eight business-class seats behind a small galley/boarding area, which looked like a good option for a more intimate experience.

The seats fold down to 75 inches in length to become fully flat beds, though the footwell is a bit narrow.

Cathay Pacific gave out British lifestyle brand Bamford amenity kits that had moisturizer, cooling body gel, pillow mist, an eye mask, earplugs, a toothbrush and toothpaste and mouthwash. There were also noise-canceling headphones and a bottle of water at the seat.

The seat had lots of little storage areas, along with slippers (but no pajamas, as Cathay only has pajamas on select planes with first class).

Bathrooms are plentiful, with two in the front of the main business-class cabin and one more behind. The coolest thing was that the two bathrooms in front have windows — something you don't see that often on airplanes. Amenities were provided by Bamford and included a moisturizing spray and lotion.

The inflight entertainment was great, with an 18.5-inch HD touchscreen and plenty of movies and entertainment. I was able to choose from hundreds of movies and television shows (including a documentary on Cathay Pacific's 80th anniversary). There was also a tail camera and a moving map. A handheld controller is available to navigate the screen.

Cathay Pacific provides free Wi-Fi for business-class passengers, and I found it worked well on my flight. It's not as fast as Starlink, but it was still easy for me to get some work done.

I really like Cathay Pacific's business-class seats on these planes, though I'm excited to try one of Cathay's newer Aria Suite business-class products someday. Those suites are currently being installed on their Boeing 777-300ER fleet.

I'm especially hoping to see it on flights to and from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), which the airline has hinted could come as soon as next year. (The timing of that rollout remains to be confirmed.)

A friendly and attentive crew, delicious food and good bedding made for a great flight across the Pacific. I had especially good service with flight attendants Mei, Amanda and Elsa, all of whom were super friendly and chatty.

Service wasn't as formal as some Asian airlines I've flown, and the crew was fun to be around.

A predeparture beverage of orange juice or water was served during boarding.

Not long after takeoff, flight attendants served drinks. I went with a nonalcoholic Cathay Delight, the airline's signature nonalcoholic drink, made with kiwi, coconut and mint.

That was followed by a lovely amuse-bouche of a deviled egg. I could have happily eaten 20 of them.

The egg dish was served with a Betsy Free, Cathay Pacific's nonalcoholic version of its signature Betsy beer, in a vintage-style Cathay Pacific beer can.

That was followed by an absolutely delicious lunch: a roast carrot soup with a selection of breads, a hearty buffalo mozzarella and rocket pesto salad with grilled radicchio and toasted hazelnuts, and a roasted chicken breast in a maple-chipotle barbecue sauce, served with corn on the cob, creamed spinach and garlic mashed potatoes.

The dessert cart was filled with things like cheese and fruit plates, a yogurt panna cotta, ice cream, or a raspberry tiramisu and, of course, port or wine.

The flight attendants saw me snapping a ton of pictures, so they ended up letting me sample a little bit of almost everything. What a feast!

As if that weren't enough, flight attendants later brought around a chocolate sampler.

There were also snacks set out in the area between the two business-class cabins.

I was able to pre-select a second meal before the flight, and went with a classic beef burger.

There was a nice set of options available on the pre-order menu.

That meal was served after I'd gotten a few hours of shut-eye. Cathay Pacific is well-known for its burgers, and this one didn't disappoint.

I'm not sure how they managed to make a burger served at 30,000 feet taste good, but they did.

The flight attendants helped make my bed with a Bamford-branded mattress pad, duvet and large pillow. I managed to get about five hours of sleep — not too bad.

Before landing, there was yet another meal.

Breakfast was a more traditional Chinese meal of congee with shrimp dumplings and siu mai. Honestly, at that point, I was so full that I didn't eat much of it, but I did enjoy about four cappuccinos.

I'll tell you one thing: Come hungry when flying international on Cathay Pacific.

I was able to score that business-class seat on Cathay Pacific's newly resumed flight to Hong Kong for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in federal security tax. You can also book Cathay flights with American Airlines AAdvantage miles.

Unfortunately, low-level award space has been increasingly hard to come by using partners lately. That's why I always look when a new or newly resumed route goes on sale. I've often found low-level awards when the route first comes up for booking.

That also happened recently when American Airlines announced new service to Prague and newly resumed flights to Budapest,. The airline made business-class redemptions widely available for just 55,000 Alaska Atmos Rewards points.

So when a new route starts or resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

Related: 9 flight award booking hacks every traveler should know

Of course, you'll likely find more availability using Cathay Pacific's own program: Asia Miles. Cathay Pacific often releases more award availability to its own members. You can transfer miles 1:1 from multiple Cathay Pacific banking partners — including Bilt and Citi ThankYou Rewards, among others — directly to Asia Miles. American Express Membership Rewards also transfers to Asia Miles but at a reduced 5:4 ratio.

Award search tools are increasingly a big part of my deal hunt. Some of my favorites include Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel. I also rely on the Points Path award tool, which runs in my browser, so I can see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

Flexibility is another key to finding award availability like this. You'll often need to travel whenever a seat is available, not on a specific date. If you're open to multiple destinations, you'll also have better luck finding the cheapest awards, especially to destinations like Asia. Consider using wherever you find the best redemption as a jumping-off point to see other destinations in the region.

Business class on Cathay Pacific's A350-900s may not have all the excitement of its newer Aria Suite, but it's still a super-compelling product, as my recent flight from Seattle to Hong Kong showed. This trip proved once again why Cathay Pacific is one of my favorite airlines, and the newly resumed service from Seattle adds another option for American travelers.

Friendly service, a great seat, and incredible food and beverages made this trip one to remember. The best part was getting all that for just 75,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points.

Keep an eye out for newly launched (or relaunched) routes when you are looking for your next great redemption. You might get a happy surprise.
