#6021. What a Hormuz Endgame Could Actually Look Like

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: What a Hormuz Endgame Could Actually Look Like

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

With the prospect of renewed war in Iran seemingly off the table for now, and given the Trump administration’s redoubled commitment to economic pressure to overwhelm Tehran, the question again becomes: What will be the fate of the Strait of Hormuz?

U.S. President Donald Trump, despite earlier threats to reignite hostilities in a last bid to cow Iran’s resistance, appears to have parked the military option. U.S. Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio also indicated that the double-whammy of Operation Economic Outcast (a naval blockade) and Iron Gate (a land blockade of Iranian trade) will bend the regime to the administration’s will. Not even angry phone calls with Israeli leadership appear able to summon the dogs of war again.

With the prospect of renewed war in Iran seemingly off the table for now, and given the Trump administration’s redoubled commitment to economic pressure to overwhelm Tehran, the question again becomes: What will be the fate of the Strait of Hormuz?

U.S. President Donald Trump, despite earlier threats to reignite hostilities in a last bid to cow Iran’s resistance, appears to have parked the military option. U.S. Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio also indicated that the double-whammy of Operation Economic Outcast (a naval blockade) and Iron Gate (a land blockade of Iranian trade) will bend the regime to the administration’s will. Not even angry phone calls with Israeli leadership appear able to summon the dogs of war again.

That means that the overarching question—beyond the fate of Iran’s previously “obliterated” nuclear program, something that does not seem amenable to short-term diplomacy—is who will control the most strategic waterway on Earth.

Before the war, which began in February, the Strait of Hormuz saw the transit of 20 percent of all seaborne oil exports in the world. It was never closed before, though there was a “tanker war” in the 1980s during the Iran-Iraq conflict that disrupted regional energy flows. But the strait was closed for much of this year, and it has only been prized open at great cost in recent months by the efforts of the U.S. Navy and the fortitude and deep pockets of seafarers and shipping companies. Oil flows out of Hormuz, and indeed the broader Middle East, are as high now, on average, as they were before the war began. Coupled with dovish talk from Washington, the global price of oil has plummeted in recent weeks from $114 a barrel to the low $90s.

But that does not portend a return to normal. Shipping rates have fallen from their sky-high levels earlier this autumn, but they remain multiples of their prewar prices. Iran continues to target and strike tankers and other vessels that transit the strait, with two incidents in just the last 24 hours.

Oil flows from the Persian Gulf—just not freely.

Any negotiated end to the now nine-month conflict will have to confront the future navigational regime of the Strait of Hormuz. That was a question on which the July memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran punted, but it cannot be forever forestalled. On the one hand, what suddenly became Iran’s greatest strategic asset—a chokehold over the world’s carotid artery—will not be surrendered summarily. On the other hand, it is a wasting asset and will diminish further in the years to come. Saudi Arabia has expanded its overland pipelines to bypass the strait, as has the United Arab Emirates, meaning the constricted and vulnerable seaborne route is less critical.

“The strait is an asset of declining value for Iran,” said James Kraska, a professor of maritime law at the U.S. Naval War College.

Kraska has some thoughts on how to chart a course to a sustainable future for the Strait of Hormuz, drawing on international law, lessons from previous big-power showdowns, and current straits-management regimes in other parts of the world, including the Strait of Malacca. He laid them out in some detail earlier this year.

The thrust of the argument for his “Hormuz Declaration” is a recognition that Iran, after the war, will want to retain some measure of control over a vital chokepoint of the world economy, but it cannot be the sole arbiter. Iran and Oman, which share the territorial waters that shrink into the narrows of Hormuz, will need to be at the forefront of any postwar agreement. But it must also be backed by major powers that rely on the waterway, including China, the United States, and Europe.

But the continued shortfall of refined products means little relief at the pump.

Washington and Tehran are grappling over a “memorandum of misunderstanding.”

Ships can’t navigate a reality that exists only in Trump’s head.

What that would mean in practical terms is a return to the prewar situation in which ships pass through the center of the strait, free of threats or tariffs, rather than skirting toward the Iranian or Omani coasts as at present, under the threat of drones, mines, and missiles.

Iran’s plan for a tollbooth in the strait, which would charge passing tankers millions of dollars and potentially bring in billions of dollars in annual revenue, is a bad idea, Kraska argued. A richer vein could be tapped by Tehran gaining access to frozen assets and reentering the global economy, something sorely needed for an economy facing a dearth of imports and inflation of around 140 percent a year.

“I believe that what I’ve offered is the start of a framework, a Hormuz Declaration, and a cooperative mechanism. And that’s really the only way—but it will require Iran to feel it gets enough to give it room to negotiate,” Kraska said. “The material benefits of a deal are evident for both sides, and there’s a face-saving way for Iran to do that.”

Under the current situation, oil from most Gulf countries largely gets out, one way or the other, while oil exports from Iran have all but collapsed. A negotiated, international regime for the management of Hormuz would bring down costs for all oil exporters and return Iran’s oil to global markets.

The immediate obstacle to such a deal is that Iran appears determined to insist on compliance with the conditions that Trump signed off on over the summer, including an end to the naval blockade, the end of U.S. military presence in the region, and an end to fighting in other theaters such as Lebanon.

The United States, for its part, has never been keen on granting Iran any veto power over Hormuz in the postwar landscape, even though a return to the status quo ante is now impossible. That standoff explains why oil remains above $90 a barrel despite an end to major combat operations in the region.

U.S. officials believe that sustained economic pressure on Iran will buckle Iran’s leadership, which has spent nearly half a century battling sanctions and international isolation. Kraska is not so sure. The new normal may be a war-not-war that keeps markets on edge and prices relatively high but never resolves into either peace or escalation.

“The most likely indication of what is to come in the near future is what is in the present, which is mowing the grass, basically,” Kraska said. “I just think we will continue to muddle through over the next year or two and never get a final resolution. Because we’ve seen with Iran that even when you get a resolution, there’s a compliance problem.”

Keith Johnson is a staff writer at Foreign Policy covering geoeconomics and energy. Bluesky: @kfj-fp.bsky.social X: @KFJ_FP

#6019. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

In South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

Democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with new congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

With GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

Under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

And one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

Among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

Rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

#6017. Van Hollen announces bid for majority leader, but Schumer says he has the votes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader.

Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Schumer has already said he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer said in a statement.

Schumer’s supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

“The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management,” Baldwin said. “The same is true in the Senate.”

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

“Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”

Van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year’s budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

“We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people,” Van Hollen said. “We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. … We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage.”

He also said he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Van Hollen’s early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed said in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”

#6016. Hound Dogs, Driftwood, High Art Ninjas, and Is That a Corkscrew on Steroids?

As long as you’ve got good taste, you’ll find lots to like as the Art Dealers Association fair returns after a year’s hiatus.

Tennessee artists get a well-deserved spot on the ADAA marquee Left: Jared Small, Chrysanthemum–Peach, 2026. Right: Jared Small, Copper Ivy–Peach, 2026.

’T is the season for buying and selling and looking and being seen, so I visited the opening extravaganza of the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA) on Thursday with red-letter curiosity. It’s always good, and I’ve always reviewed it for NR except last year, when it was canceled in July, booth deposits returned, and it went missing from the art season for the first time since 1989, the year that the 200-strong national group, the art-dealer trade association, had its first splashy fair.

“A strategic pause,” the ADAA’s board said in an email, meant to give it time to “reimagine” The Art Show — the fair’s formal name — “with long-term sustainability and member value in mind.” They said it wasn’t money, though it’s nearly always about money, and in 2025 the mid-level art market seemed grim. Well, the fair’s back, at the Park Avenue Armory as always, and the booths seem smaller and more modern in content.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

’T is the season for buying and selling and looking and being seen, so I visited the opening extravaganza of the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA) on Thursday with red-letter curiosity. It’s always good, and I’ve always reviewed it for NR except last year, when it was canceled in July, booth deposits returned, and it went missing from the art season for the first time since 1989, the year that the 200-strong national group, the art-dealer trade association, had its first splashy fair.

“A strategic pause,” the ADAA’s board said in an email, meant to give it time to “reimagine” The Art Show — the fair’s formal name — “with long-term sustainability and member value in mind.” They said it wasn’t money, though it’s nearly always about money, and in 2025 the mid-level art market seemed grim. Well, the fair’s back, at the Park Avenue Armory as always, and the booths seem smaller and more modern in content.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

Argument: Congress Must Stop Arming Israel

Analysts have spent much time over the past week trying to explain the “blue tsunami” that swept the United States during the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Democrats gained historic majorities in both the House and Senate, teeing up for a confrontational two years with President Donald Trump.

Many voters clearly wanted their elected officials to stop writing blank checks for Israel and to end the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. About 6 in 10 U.S. voters told an Associated Press election survey that attacking Iran was the wrong decision. A Chicago Council poll found that 68 percent of Americans said the war had not been worth its costs. According to the same study, 56 percent favored reducing or eliminating U.S. military aid to Israel. The Chicago Council also reported that 57 percent of Americans backed restrictions to prevent U.S. military aid from supporting Israeli operations against Palestinians.

Analysts have spent much time over the past week trying to explain the “blue tsunami” that swept the United States during the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Democrats gained historic majorities in both the House and Senate, teeing up for a confrontational two years with President Donald Trump.

Many voters clearly wanted their elected officials to stop writing blank checks for Israel and to end the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. About 6 in 10 U.S. voters told an Associated Press election survey that attacking Iran was the wrong decision. A Chicago Council poll found that 68 percent of Americans said the war had not been worth its costs. According to the same study, 56 percent favored reducing or eliminating U.S. military aid to Israel. The Chicago Council also reported that 57 percent of Americans backed restrictions to prevent U.S. military aid from supporting Israeli operations against Palestinians.

The White House appears to have taken notice. Vice President J.D. Vance wrote on X that “the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. … The reason we lost is the war.” He also cited the desire to “change our relationship to Israel” as a factor in some Trump voters choosing to back Democrats.

Discussing Republicans’ loss, Trump himself admitted to the Wall Street Journal that “Iran was a piece of it.” And in an apparent acknowledgment that supporting U.S. military aid to Israel carried a political cost, Trump announced on Election Day that the United States would end the $3.8 billion in annual military aid to the country by the end of this calendar year. Trump later told 60 Minutes that “there is a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.”

Trump’s announcement marks a watershed moment in U.S. foreign policy. But U.S. aid to Israel won’t end with a phone call. The current U.S.-Israel military aid agreement runs through fiscal year 2028; Trump did not explain how the United States would halt funding sooner. What’s more, cutting Israel’s annual U.S. military aid package would still leave room for supplemental military funding. It also would not stop Israel from buying American weapons through government sales and commercial contracts.

For Israeli authorities and their supporters, maintaining the flow of U.S. arms to Israel is far more important than who pays for them. If Israel—rather than U.S. taxpayers—pays for a bomb, that does not mitigate the bomb’s impact when Israel drops it on a Palestinian family. The United States will remain complicit in Israeli genocide and apartheid as long as U.S. arms keep flowing.

The new Congress should end all U.S. arms transfers to Israel. It can start by removing the $3.8 billion in military aid from fiscal 2027 appropriations and by blocking supplemental military funding. The House has already passed a spending bill that earmarks these billions in arms for Israel. Congress must remove that earmark before the appropriations bill becomes law.

Lawmakers should also prohibit new arms sales and deliveries to Israel under existing contracts, commercial export licenses, and stockpile arrangements. Congress should ensure full transparency around U.S. military aid and both government and commercial sales to Israel, as some information is not public. Voters deserve to know whether the U.S. government has truly stopped the flow of arms to Israel or simply tweaked the mechanisms by which Israel receives them.

It is critical, too, that Congress strike Section 219 from the House-passed National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal 2027. The provision would expand military cooperation with Israel through joint weapons development and production. In particular, the provision would direct the Defense Department to designate an executive agent to expand military technology cooperation with the country. Section 219 promotes joint ventures, co-production, and integration of jointly developed or Israeli-origin technology into U.S. military systems.

Congress should also reject Republican Rep. Don Bacon’s H.R. 10796 bill, which would advance a similar initiative. Pentagon co-production preserves the machinery that enables Israeli abuses—without the safeguards that Congress wrote into law to prevent the United States from arming repressive regimes.

Finally, the Senate should adopt Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s resolution drawing on Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, which bars security assistance to any government engaged in a consistent pattern of gross human rights violations. If approved, the resolution would force the State Department to submit, within 30 days, a report covering abuses against Americans and Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. On Sept. 29, 47 senators, including all but one Democrat, supported a motion to advance the resolution, but 51 voted against it. The resolution thus failed.

If the new Senate adopts the resolution, then the State Department would be required to write such a report. If the department misses the 30-day deadline to do so, Section 502B would bar delivery of U.S. security assistance to Israel until the State Department delivers a report that finds that Israel is not engaged in a consistent pattern of human rights abuses. Congress can also use Section 502B’s procedures to restrict or terminate assistance through legislation. The statute covers not only military aid, but also arms sales and licenses for defense exports.

Van Hollen has emerged a potential challenger to Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Having a principled voice such as his in a leadership role would pave the way for a broader change in U.S. policy toward Israel and send a clear message that the Democratic Party understands the mandate that it just received from the American people.

Regardless of who takes up the reins in the Senate, Congress should pass a joint war powers resolution directing an end to the Iran war, which the United States has waged alongside Israel since February. Congress should pair that measure with legislation prohibiting funds for continued or expanded U.S. military operations on Iran, covering both direct military spending and emergency transfers to Israel.

The Trump administration continues to send mixed messages about the direction of the war, but after a classified October briefing, Sen. Chris Murphy described the U.S. military plan as “insane.” A war of this magnitude—which has killed, maimed, and displaced thousands of civilians and also damaged infrastructure and economies across the Middle East—has been left to Trump’s whims for too long.

On both Israel and Iran, the American people have spoken: They want Congress to reassert its critical constitutional role and end the fighting. Now legislators must act.

Omar Shakir is the executive director of Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN). A human rights lawyer focused on the Middle East and U.S. foreign policy, he previously served as the Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch. X: @OmarSShakir

Florida narrowly missed the quake, with Republicans winning all the major statewide races by the thinnest of margins. The one-time quintessential purple state, a so-goes-the-nation bellwether with a relatively even amount of registered Republicans and Democrats, turned remarkably red in the Trump era following Barack Obamaâs back-to-back wins in 2008 and 2012. The state legislature redrew its maps to enshrine a supermajority, and a post-Covid influx of GOP transplants seeking lower taxes and lax regulations shifted the balance significantly. A Democrat hasnât made a fight of the governorâs race this decade, and no Democratic Senate candidate has come close to winning since Bill Nelson lost his reelection bid in 2018.

Angie Nixon felt different. The Jacksonville organizer and bookstore owner ran a proudly democratic socialist campaign, advocating for universal healthcare in a state beset by multiple insurance crises and affordability issues. Her polls looked good up to Election Day, and on Tuesday night, victories across the country made her race in the Sunshine State look winnable. Ultimately though, Nixon could not replicate the victories of other rabble-rousers like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas. She lost to incumbent Ashley Moody, who was appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to fill the seat left vacant by Marco Rubioâs confirmation as secretary of state, by less than two percentage points. Moody outspent Nixon by more than double to barely eke out a majority.Â

The Florida Democratic Party deserves some blame for being woefully behind the times. After a 2019 squeaker between DeSantis and the progressive Andrew Gillum, the party moved as fast as it could from any candidate that might excite its base. They ran a former Republican for governor in each of the last two gubernatorial races, no doubt depressing turnout and enthusiasm among the Democratic base with their moderate picks.Â

But a close look at the rest of the Florida races reveals the culprit in Nixonâs narrow loss. Despite a gerrymander meant to calcify Republican supermajorities in the state and a political stiff in the form of David Jolly at the top of the ballot for governor, the GOP lost seats in the state legislature. The energy in Florida and, remarkably, throughout the South, was with anyone running against Republicans. The blame for Nixonâs defeat lies almost solely with national Democrats and their stubborn refusal to back Nixon with either messaging or money.Â

Since her shock primary win in August, Nixon has complained about Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee recalcitrance to anyone who will listen. In September, she told MS NOW hosts Symone Sanders Townsend and Eugene Daniels that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was less than thrilled about her race.

âWhen I did speak with Sen. Schumer on the phone, it was basically a âwe will see,ââ she said. âHeâs going to look into it. Thatâs what was said, that heâs going to look into it.â

Nixon went on to say that Democrats were wary of throwing in behind a Black woman in the South following Kamala Harrisâ 2024 loss: âFolks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President Harris lost as a Black woman, and so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South.â

In later interviews, she claimed that national Democrats wrote off Florida in advance, declining to put money behind her candidacy because they believe the state is âracist.âÂ

The pale blue dots on Floridaâs election map tell the story. The democratic socialist was able to win in Miami-Dade County, despite a Cuban-American population that shudders at anything that sounds like revolution. On the other end of the state, typically Republican Jacksonville swung to the left. An enthusiastic push in the stateâs timidly liberal cities could have narrowed the gap in favor of Nixon and added tens of thousands of votes to her final total. According to analysis by Wesleyan Media Project, the national party and affiliated PACs spent 10 advertising dollars in Iowa for every one they spent in Florida in the raceâs final weeks, and it showed. The Hawkeye State now has a new Democratic governor-elect and senator-elect.

It was the same story throughout the South. Democrats overperformed in states where the national party bothered to fight.

Blue Texas became a reality because of seemingly unlimited spending â it was the most expensive Senate race in history âÂ and national messaging hits on behalf of Talarico. Louisiana and Mississippi offered two incredibly close Senate races in states long assumed to be GOP strongholds. In Louisiana, Democrat Jamie Davis lost to Republican Julia Letlow by only two points. As New York Times contributing opinion writer Steven Rattner pointed out, Davis kept the race close despite receiving zero advertising dollars from the national party in October, per the WMPâs analysis.

#6012. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing “regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce’s role that raises national security concerns.”

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don’t let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don’t get sold to them, even though it’s the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can’t access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you’re going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

#6011. Serbia’s Student Movement Faces Its Next Test

Analysis: Serbia’s Student Movement Faces Its Next Test

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

For nearly two years, student protesters demanded a fundamental transformation of Serbia’s political system, and the Oct. 25 elections marked an extraordinary step toward achieving it. Their movement defeated the formidable political machine of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a stunning upset.

The Student List secured approximately 53 percent of the vote and 140 parliamentary seats, with a record voter turnout of nearly 70 percent. It ended 14 years of uninterrupted rule by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is left with 103 seats. A new government must be formed within 90 days of the official results.

For nearly two years, student protesters demanded a fundamental transformation of Serbia’s political system, and the Oct. 25 elections marked an extraordinary step toward achieving it. Their movement defeated the formidable political machine of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a stunning upset.

The Student List secured approximately 53 percent of the vote and 140 parliamentary seats, with a record voter turnout of nearly 70 percent. It ended 14 years of uninterrupted rule by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is left with 103 seats. A new government must be formed within 90 days of the official results.

The victory is remarkable not least because the students disregarded almost every convention of electoral politics. They rejected traditional parties, eschewed recognizable leadership, and offered voters something closer to a moral crusade than a normal political program. The elections therefore functioned less as a choice between competing platforms and more as a referendum on Vucic’s years in power.

Winning power and exercising it are different things. The qualities that made the student movement effective in opposition—from the students’ status as political outsiders to their ideological heterogeneity—could become liabilities in government. Now, the Student List must prove to an expectant public that it can move beyond deliberating what needs to change and govern.

Serbia’s ongoing political upheaval traces back to November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed outside the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station, killing 16 people. Initial demonstrations demanded government accountability for the disaster and transparency over who was responsible for the construction and how public funds were spent.

As protests spread across Serbia, the disaster became a symbol of broader anger over endemic corruption, political patronage, and the ruling party’s stranglehold on state institutions. The movement evolved into a campaign for wholesale political change, culminating in snap parliamentary elections. Students, who carried out university occupations and demonstrations that put immense pressure on Vucic’s government, were the driving force.

The students’ grassroots efforts had structural advantages. The movement was decentralized, operating through network-based university groups that made it difficult for the government to identify leaders it could discredit or co-opt. The students also rejected Serbia’s opposition establishment, whose chronic infighting, electoral failures, and tainted reputation made it an unappealing alternative to Vucic. This helped the movement attract support from across the political spectrum.

The students initially insisted their objective was to compel Serbia’s institutions to function better rather than to enter electoral politics. But after six months of protest, they began to recognize the limitations of their approach. At the time, I argued in Foreign Policy that street demonstrations alone would not transform Serbia, and that the students would have to turn to the ballot box to achieve lasting change. In May 2025, they took that step, demanding snap elections.

Vucic resisted calls for an early vote for another 16 months before finally dissolving parliament on Sept. 9 and scheduling the October elections. He resigned as president to contest the election as the SNS candidate for prime minister, temporarily handing the position to parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabic. (Serbia must hold an early presidential election by Dec. 27.)

So, the students did enter politics—though on unique and even inadvisable terms. Rather than joining forces with established parties, they assembled the Student List, an electoral coalition that included academics, professionals, and political newcomers. Candidates were nominated and vetted by student plenums at individual university faculties, which agreed on a final list through a nationwide process of collective decision-making.

The Student List retained a horizontal structure and avoided elevating a charismatic leader, consciously rejecting the political culture that Vucic cultivated. That strategy was an enormous gamble. The students bet that public dissatisfaction was widespread enough to bring habitual nonvoters to the polls: primarily politically disengaged Serbians, first-time voters, and people who had become disillusioned with electoral politics in the Vucic era.

But they did not have an obvious plan for winning over the government’s supporters, many of whom had a material stake in Vucic’s patronage system. SNS reportedly has more than 700,000 members; party loyalty is often a prerequisite for securing public-sector employment. In smaller towns where the state is a major employer, supporting the ruling party is therefore as much a matter of economic self-preservation as political conviction.

While in power, the SNS cultivated and invested in preserving the status quo, which included public-sector employees, business owners benefiting from state contracts, and older voters who credited Vucic with rising pensions and economic stability.

Vucic campaigned on his economic record and sought to discredit the student movement, accusing its supporters of attempting a so-called color revolution and portraying their slate of inexperienced candidates as a threat. His message was familiar: The SNS delivered stability, infrastructure investment, and higher wages, pensions, and living standards. Serbia has experienced genuine economic development under Vucic, but as elsewhere, the rising cost of living has strained household finances.

By contrast, the student movement asked voters to embrace uncertainty for the promise of a better future. Its 11-point reform agenda promised to restore the rule of law and respect for the constitution, free the judiciary from political interference, confiscate illegally acquired wealth, and dismantle the patronage networks that have permeated state institutions.

The SNS campaign rested on what it thought was a straightforward calculation: Would voters risk their livelihoods on an inexperienced opposition promising to tear down the existing order? This underestimated how much public tolerance for Vucic had deteriorated. His party is plagued by allegations of corruption, cronyism, and abuses of authority; the touted stability increasingly appeared to serve a small elite.

Vucic’s government also overestimated its traditional methods of intimidation. International election observers documented voter pressure, misuse of state resources, and unequal campaign conditions. Pro-government forces dominated airtime and broadcast overwhelmingly negative coverage of the Student List, according to the European Center for Research, Transparency, and Accountability. These tactics still failed to prevent the opposition from large-scale mobilization.

Ultimately, the Student List won the public’s vote, with its perceived weaknesses serving as strengths. By rejecting the established opposition, it avoided inheriting the baggage of politicians who had repeatedly failed in challenging Vucic. Its lack of obvious ideological identity united voters with otherwise incompatible convictions, and its refusal to appoint a dominant leader deprived the government of an obvious individual to demonize.

The victory of the Student List bears comparison with that of Prime Minister Peter Magyar in neighboring Hungary’s elections in April. Both movements capitalized on exhaustion with entrenched governments that blurred the distinction between party and state and turned discontent with corruption into a broader rejection of the political order.

But there is an important difference. Magyar—a former member of longtime Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s party—offered Hungary a recognizable alternative built around his leadership, combining institutional accountability with a message about deteriorating public services and living standards. Serbia’s student movement offered something more radical: an opportunity to replace the political culture itself.

The question now is whether a movement assembled around opposition to one leader can develop the coherence necessary to govern without him. The Student List’s parliamentary majority should allow it to form a government without coalition partners. But the movement has yet to settle elementary questions of leadership, including who will become prime minister and how to reconcile ideologically diverse factions.

Ilija Srdanovic, a physician and professor who became the lead candidate on the electoral list, confirmed that government appointments will be decided collectively by lawmakers, while the student plenums that elected them intend to retain an oversight role. But this risks creating competing centers of authority—a tension that is already surfacing. The Student List lawmakers and the plenums are currently deliberating how to balance the grassroots participation that defined the movement with the elected representatives’ practical need to make decisions quickly.

The Student List also encompasses left-wing academics, liberal reformers, and conservative nationalists whose different positions on key foreign-policy issues that have long been political third rails in Serbia—such as Kosovo’s independence, support for Russia, and Serbia’s European integration—could prove especially difficult to reconcile in government.

Another immediate challenge is the presidential election that is due by the end of next month. The Student List must put forward a credible candidate while simultaneously forming a government. Defeat could leave it sharing power with a hostile president, further complicating its ambitious reform plans. The scale of the October upset makes a student victory likely, however. Those who voted for the Student List likely won’t want a president who throws sand in the gears of the parliament they mobilized to elect.

The new leadership will face enormous practical obstacles to governance. SNS loyalists remain embedded throughout the state bureaucracy, where they could obstruct reforms and frustrate corruption investigations that the new government intends to pursue. Particularly challenging will be reforming the police and intelligence services, whose senior officials have been accused of surveilling and intimidating government opponents, as well as links to organized crime.

Dismantling these networks requires more than moral conviction. It demands administrative competence, political discipline, and the ability to distinguish legitimate reform from politically motivated retribution. This last distinction is particularly important. The new government will face intense pressure to deliver accountability for years of alleged abuses, and the Student List has already called on judges and prosecutors to either pursue corruption cases or resign. But indiscriminately purging the state apparatus risks the sort of politicization that the students promised to end.

Equally, the new leadership cannot neglect Serbians’ material concerns. A government devoted to prosecuting its predecessor while failing to improve ordinary lives might find that enthusiasm for political renewal has a limited shelf life. Concerns are emerging about the Student List’s vague economic program, with economists questioning its investment plans. An approaching budget deadline will quickly test the new government’s economic credibility.

It would also be foolish to write Vucic off. The SNS retains 103 parliamentary seats, extensive patronage networks, and influence over local administrations and media outlets. Vucic has already vowed to return to power, though he must first keep his political machine intact. Vucic has been involved in national politics since 1993; he spent 12 years in opposition after the fall of Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. He will not simply disappear.

Dismantling an entrenched political system is one thing, but building a functioning alternative is another. The students have won an impressive mandate, but their sweeping ambitions will take more than one parliamentary term. They must learn not only how to win elections but also how to retain voters’ confidence. That demands a transition from protest to politics, from moral absolutism to compromise, and from opposition to responsibility.

Serbia’s student movement accomplished something that many people believed impossible: They ended an era of political dominance through the ballot box. Now, their task is to demonstrate that they can build something better in its place.

Aleks Eror is a journalist and political consultant from Belgrade. His work has been published by the Financial Times, UnHerd, and other publications. X: @slandr

#6010. Taika Waititi’s Instagram crash out is a Trumpian sore loss

For all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some important lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal government’s medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if we’re not careful, we’re all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

Waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Donald Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that “Klara and the Sun” was “rebounding” with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the film’s 25% critics score. (For what it’s worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a film’s quality.) “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,” Waititi captioned the post. “But I do listen to the people . . . Let’s spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”

Reading Waititi’s emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trump’s favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a “SAD!” at the end of Waititi’s caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trump’s poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, “The critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.”)

Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititi’s caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trump’s agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesday’s midterms. But judging by the results, MAGA’s influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended — at least for now.

Not to be all, “Oh, won’t someone think of the celebrities?” about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that it’s bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

One would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, “Jojo Rabbit,” which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propaganda’s influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititi’s writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: It’s downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics — people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi — just six years later.

But this is the rot that social media creates. Whether it’s Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.

For some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the month’s salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today — to pursue one’s passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one — is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesn’t stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a new project after a string of flops.

If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

What Waititi fails to realize is that he’s not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But that’s hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social media’s effect on human behavior, it’s had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyone’s a critic, then no one is, and that’s precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like they’re poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

But it’s not just Waititi who’s vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether it’s a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer tech’s sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. I’ve seen this affect critics’ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

What’s most concerning in Waititi’s response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before it’s even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other people’s perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion shows maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger won’t do anything for a person’s growth, artistic or otherwise. America’s politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

If America’s blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerberg’s Instagram, we owe some props to one of the century’s most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” actually got a few things right. In last month’s companion piece to “The Social Network,” Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his director’s eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. “I’m worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts you can’t learn,” he admitted.

While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkin’s introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

about how and where politics and film overlap

#6008. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.
